article_content: Al Jazeera has declined to broadcast video footage received from suspected French attacker Mohammed Merah, stating it violates the networkâs Code of Ethics. The network also refused all requests for copies of the material, announcing its decision on Twitter. The video, delivered by mail on a USB drive, contains graphic scenes of the March 2012 shootings in Toulouse and Montauban â including gunshots, the cries of victims, religious chants, and Quranic passages. According to Al Jazeeraâs Paris bureau chief, Zied Tarrouche, the footage appears to have been recorded by a camera worn around Merahâs neck. French President Nicolas Sarkozy publicly urged all TV networks not to air the footage, calling it a matter of 'respect for the victims and the republic.' Al Jazeera handed the original USB to French authorities but retained a copy. Mohammed Merah, who killed seven people â three French soldiers, a rabbi, and three young children â was killed after a 32-hour police siege. Two others were seriously wounded. Merahâs brother, Abdelkader, was arrested and charged with complicity in the murders and terrorism-related conspiracy. His lawyer argues he is being unfairly targeted as a scapegoat since the perpetrator is deceased. Israeli officials confirmed Merah had visited Israel and the West Bank in September 2010, entering through the Allenby Bridge and undergoing questioning by Shin Bet before being allowed entry. Despite being known to French intelligence for traveling to Pakistan and Afghanistan and appearing on the U.S. no-fly list, Merah was not detained before the attacks. Prime Minister Francois Fillon stated there was insufficient evidence for pre-emptive arrest. The attacks occurred over three separate incidents: the first targeting a soldier responding to an online scooter ad; the second at a shopping center; and the third at a Jewish school, where a motorcyclist in a helmet opened fire on children and staff. Police confirmed the same weapons were used in all three attacks.

article_content: (CNN) â Slowed but not deterred by Antarctic winds exceeding 100 mph, low visibility, and heavy snow, rescuers seized improved weather conditions on Saturday to close in on the location where a plane carrying three Canadians activated an emergency beacon. The condition of the three crew members aboard the Twin Otter operated by Calgary-based Kenn Borek Air Ltd. remained unknown nearly three days after the flight went missing and rescue operations began. The aircraft was en route from the South Pole to an Italian research base at Terra Nova Bay, according to Maritime New Zealand. 'It is difficult to imagine a more challenging environment,' said Steve Rendle, spokesperson for the Rescue Coordination Centre New Zealand. The emergency beacon ceased transmitting on Thursday evening, likely due to a depleted battery â about a day after the plane was reported missing. By then, rescuers had narrowed the search area, but persistent storms prevented visual confirmation, Rendle added. Winds reached nearly 105 mph on Wednesday. One search aircraft reached a camp roughly 30 miles from the beaconâs last signal. Two helicopters were advancing toward a forward base on a glacier Saturday afternoon, while a C-130 Hercules aircraft circled the activation site seeking visual contact. 'We have a reasonably positive forecast for that location,' Rendle said from Wellington. The missing crewâs survival kit included thermal suits, mountain tents, and enough food and water for five days. The aircraft is believed to be stranded at an elevation of 13,000 feet near the summit of Mount Elizabeth in the rugged Queen Alexandra Range â a remote region far from any Antarctic base. 'We would expect them to be with the plane,' Rendle said. 'Common sense dictates staying near the beacon.' Kenn Borek Air Ltd. did not respond to a message left by CNN on Friday night. In a statement issued Wednesday, the airline confirmed the flight was overdue but did not release the crew membersâ names. According to its website, Kenn Borek Air operates one of the worldâs largest fleets of Twin Otters. 'We are best known for our remote polar services using ski-equipped Twin Otters,' the company states. 'KBAL provides a wide range of additional services, including medevac, survey flights, paradrops, float operations, and third-party maintenance and overhaul.' The Queen Alexandra Range â approximately 100 miles long â was named by Ernest Shackleton during the British Antarctic Expedition of 1907â1909. Peter West, spokesperson for the National Science Foundation, which oversees the U.S. Antarctic Program, noted that 24 hours of continuous daylight at this time of year is aiding search efforts. CNN's Dave Alsup and Erica Harrington contributed to this report.

article_content: By Rob Preece. PUBLISHED: 10:17 EST, 17 September 2012. | UPDATED: 01:52 EST, 18 September 2012. A fraudster who attempted to smuggle drugs into prison for her incarcerated boyfriend has been jailed after police discovered Â£700 worth of heroin concealed in her bra. Officers found the Class A drug in Stacey Martinâs underwear after stopping her car in Wolverhampton on April 7, 2011. Detectives believe the heroin was intended for her partner, Andrew Warley â a connection confirmed after they thwarted a nearly identical plot orchestrated by the pair just two days earlier. Martin, 32, had previously hidden a Â£360 package of skunk cannabis inside a packet of crisps near Ranby Prison in Nottinghamshire. Her plan was for an inmate on litter-picking duty to retrieve the packet and smuggle it inside for Warley, who was serving time for dangerous driving. However, police intercepted the scheme and replaced the real drugs with fake ones. Martin, of Penn, Wolverhampton, was sentenced to two years in prison after pleading guilty at Wolverhampton Crown Court to two counts of conspiracy to supply drugs and one count of conspiracy to commit fraud. The fraud charge stemmed from her staged carjacking, designed to fraudulently claim insurance money. Warley, already imprisoned, was sentenced to four and a half years after admitting to the same three charges, plus an additional count of perverting the course of justice. The carjacking scheme occurred on March 26, 2011. Witnesses reported seeing Martin pull into a petrol station in Wolverhampton in a nearly Â£40,000 BMW convertible, only for two men to rush her, steal the keys, and flee. The insurance company denied the claim after investigators uncovered that Martin had paid a Â£25,405 cash deposit for the vehicle despite having no verifiable income. On April 5, 2011, Martin was observed parking near Ranby Prison. A male associate placed the crisp packet under a tree. The next morning, undercover officers watched as an inmate on litter-picking duty picked up the packet and carried it toward the prison gate â only to be arrested upon entry. Two days later, Martin was driving a Ford Fiesta when police stopped her again. During a routine search, no drugs were found. But once at the station, she confessed: 'Iâve got it in my bra â half of brown.' Detective Constable Lee Price of West Midlands Policeâs Organised Crime Unit said: 'The pair were clearly planning ways to get drugs into prison while simultaneously attempting to defraud insurers of nearly Â£40,000 through a staged robbery of Martinâs BMW. Detectives uncovered their schemes, and both are now facing the consequences. Police, prison authorities, and the courts take any attempt to introduce drugs, phones, or contraband into jails extremely seriously â offenders risk up to 10 years in prison.'

article_content: Public scandals and White House security breaches have revealed a decline in the Secret Service, an agency that spent decades as the gold standard in law enforcement. Now, former agents and leaders who once oversaw the agency are pushing back, arguing that the Secret Service has been burdened with expanding protective dutiesâprotecting more people and handling more threatsâall while its budget has remained flat or been cut. Some lawmakers are unconvinced, asserting that the agency has been unaccountable for years and lacks proper oversight. The Secret Service has come under increasing criticism for security lapses and operational gaffes in recent years. According to The Washington Post, on September 11, 2001, the Secret Service was responsible for protecting 18 individuals, including President George W. Bush, his immediate family, the vice president, and his immediate family. After the 9/11 attacks, Bush ordered the agency to extend protection to his extended familyâincluding his four brothers and sisterâand Vice President Dick Cheneyâs adult daughters and grandchildren. President Barack Obama largely continued this policy. Today, the Secret Service protects 27 individuals, including Vice President Joe Bidenâs school-age granddaughters and Obamaâs close adviser, Valerie Jarrett, the Post reports. Each protected individual requires two to six agents per shift, with agents working two to three daily rotations to ensure 24/7 coverage. The Secret Service says it needs 1,420 Uniform Division officers to secure the White Houseâbut currently has only 1,320, according to the Post. Despite growing responsibilities, staffing levels have not kept pace. A wave of early retirements between the 1990s and 2002 resulted in 925 senior agents leaving the agency during their most productive years, the Post reports. This has contributed to severe gaps in experience and capacity. Uniform Division officers tasked with guarding the White House say they are frequently called in to work overtime on their days off due to chronic understaffing. The agency has canceled routine training sessions to keep officers current, as it cannot afford to remove them from duty. Due to budget shortfalls, the Secret Service eliminated all but three of its academy training classes, severely limiting new recruit intake. Beyond protective duties, the Secret Service is also responsible for combating counterfeiting. Since 9/11, it has taken on additional rolesâincluding monitoring online threats to financial institutions and surveilling large public events for potential terrorist activity, according to the Post. Another blow came when, post-9/11, the Secret Service was transferred from the Treasury Departmentâhistorically its well-funded homeâto the newly created Department of Homeland Security. Former agents say the move forced the agency to compete for funding against much larger entities like the Transportation Security Administration and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, each of which employs around 50,000 people, compared to the Secret Serviceâs 6,200. Meanwhile, the agencyâs budget has remained largely flatâor declined slightly. The 2013 budget was $1.5 billion, down from $1.6 billion the previous year. In response, the agency cut 300 positions. 'There was a competition for dollars in an increasingly finite budget environment,' Chris Cummiskey, a former Homeland Security official in the Obama administration, told the Post. In September 2014, Oscar Gonzalez, armed with a knife, breached the White House fence and reached the front door of the residence before being subdued. Director Julia Pierson resigned following the incident, which exposed critical failures: officers lacked proper training to respond to intruders, radios malfunctioned, and security protocols were ignored. Pierson herself had assumed leadership after the 2012 prostitution scandal in Colombia, in which several agents were dismissed for partying and hiring prostitutes during a pre-presidential visit. Despite appeals from current and former agents for more resources, some in Washington insist the agency has never lacked support and must eliminate waste. 'I donât think the Secret Service has been held accountable for the last 15 years,' said Utah Republican Congressman Jason Chaffetz. Tom Ridge, the first Secretary of Homeland Security, stated: 'The entire focus of the nation shifted after 9/11, and all federal agencies had to adjust to the new realities. That said, the Secret Service, because of its protective mission and direct ties to the White House, never suffered from a lack of resources to carry out their critical responsibilities during my time at DHS.' Earlier this month, a Homeland Security report criticized the Secret Serviceâs budget management, noting agency officials could not even provide a cost estimate for protecting the White House. 'No one has really looked at how much the mission, done right, actually costs,' the report concluded.

article_content: In Richmond, Virginia, the Virginia Historical Society has unveiled 'Unknown No Longer,' a groundbreaking online database identifying 3,200 enslaved individuals whose names were lost to history. The project, made possible by a $100,000 grant from Dominion Energy, draws from 8 million unpublished manuscripts â letters, diaries, ledgers, and farm records â donated by Virginia families since 1831. These documents, often written by enslavers as property inventories, reveal the names, occupations, birth and death dates, and owners of enslaved people â details rarely preserved because literacy was deliberately denied to the enslaved. The database, launched in September with 1,500 names and now expanded to over 3,200, is the first to compile such records across all of slaveholding Virginia, the state that held the largest enslaved population in the U.S. at the outbreak of the Civil War. Unlike other slave databases limited to plantation rolls or African names from ship manifests, 'Unknown No Longer' offers high-resolution scans of original documents alongside searchable fields including first and last names, gender, occupation, owner surname, date range, and document type. Society president Paul Levengood, a historian, described the painstaking detective work involved: 'You might find a reference to 'Amy' in one letter â then realize in another that she was not a relative, but an enslaved woman.' The database has already sparked emotional responses. Gale Carter, a high school history teacher from Indiana, traveled to attend a community workshop, saying, 'This isnât just personal â itâs professional. Itâs a model every state should follow.' Crasty Johnson, a Richmond genealogist, added, 'I need to know my history. I want to see the dots connect.' One user, 'Treebranch02,' shared: 'I think I found the owner of my great-great-great-grandfather â itâs exciting!' Meanwhile, a chilling 1858 letter from enslaver William Daniel Cabell details the sale of 43 enslaved people for $32,016, noting that Jane and her three children sold for $2,795, while her husband cried out, 'Glory to God on high, peace and good will to men on earth.' The letterâs claim that the enslaved were 'satisfied' reflects the enslaverâs distorted perspective â not the reality of forced separation and trauma. With over 80 attendees at its first workshop, the society plans three more to guide users â especially those new to genealogy â in navigating the database. As researcher Robert Payne noted, 'Finding Black ancestry is hard. This gives the next generation a foundation.' The Virginia Historical Society stresses that Virginiaâs legacy of slavery extends far beyond its borders â many African Americans across the South trace roots here, making this a national story of memory, identity, and justice. article_content: In November 2013, Apolinar Solis, a 51-year-old man who was legally blind in one eye, diabetic, and dependent on kidney dialysis, suffered a fatal fall while being escorted down a staircase at Manhattan Criminal Court. The suit further claims that emergency responders failed to apply basic first aid, such as ice to his head wound, and that the family was not notified of his hospitalization until a hospital employee reached out to them. The legal action targets both New York City and its contracted healthcare provider, Corizon Health Inc., accusing them of negligence, medical malpractice, and violating Solisâ constitutional rights. article_content: By Sam Webb. PUBLISHED: 14:00 EST, 9 July 2013. | UPDATED: 05:55 EST, 10 July 2013. Grief: Christopher and Lisa Avery-Wright after the inquest into the death of their son, William, outside Worth School in West Sussex, where he was a pupil. The father of a public schoolboy has criticized his school for announcing his sonâs death to other parents before informing him. William Avery-Wright, 13, died after being struck by a 4x4 while crossing the road to play rugby. His father, Christopher Avery-Wright, said Worth Schoolânear Turners Hill, Crawley, West Sussexâsent an email to parents shortly after William was injured. About half an hour later, another email, sent without his knowledge, announced Williamâs deathâwhile Mr. Avery-Wright was still unaware, traveling by train from London. As he traveled, Mr. Avery-Wright began receiving condolence texts from parents who had received the schoolâs email. Williamâs mother, Lisa Avery-Wright, had already arrived at the hospital but was advised not to tell her husband until he arrived. Following an inquest into his death, Mr. Avery-Wright condemned the school, calling its actions 'appallingly inappropriate' and saying they caused 'incredible pain.' The family is suing the school, where William excelled in cricket, rugby, and football, arguing he should have been supervised while crossing the road. The Roman Catholic school, which also posted a statement on its website, previously claimed it released the information in 'good faith,' believing both parents had been notifiedâa claim later found to be incorrect. At the two-day inquest at Crawley Town Hall, West Sussex Assistant Deputy Coroner Bridget Dolan recorded a verdict of accidental death. She did not address the schoolâs communication failures in her closing remarks, stating the focus was on the crash events, the schoolâs crossing policy, and subsequent changes. Ms. Dolan ruled out claims of neglect but noted the schoolâs rules had not been 'adhered to.' Outside court, Mr. Avery-Wright said: 'They decided to announce to the school parents by email that William had died. It caused incredible pain. If a child dies in the schoolâs custody, there should be reconciliationâand we feel the school behaved appallingly.' He added: 'When I was picked up by police at 4:30 p.m., I started receiving texts saying William had diedâI had no idea if it was true. It wasnât until 5:30 p.m., when I reached the hospital and saw my wife, that my worst fears were confirmed.' The inquest heard that William was crossing the road with a friend when he was hit by a Land Rover Defender driven by Graham Voller, who was traveling at approximately 40 mph in a 60 mph zone. Voller said he saw William suddenly appear in front of the vehicle and applied emergency brakes. He will not face criminal charges. William, a talented athlete who played golf at county level, was pronounced dead from multiple injuries at East Surrey Hospital on November 30, 2011. His friend, who was with him at the time, told police he 'froze' and was in 'disbelief.' He recalled seeing William stop and say, 'Oh my God,' just before the collision. He said they had crossed the road unsupervised before and were never required to wait for staff. Alan Mitchell, head of games at Worth School, testified that pupils in Years 7 and 8 were required to be escorted across the roadâbut the policy did not specify procedures for late students. He said policies were communicated via annual health and safety talks and reminders by housemasters. Headmaster Gino Carminati acknowledged that Paddockhurst Road was among the schoolâs top 10 risk areas. He confirmed the policy required adult supervision for younger pupils but admitted enforcement was inconsistent. Some students were unaware of the rule. Since Williamâs death, the school has banned unsupervised crossings, installed a temporary crossing, and is constructing a footbridgeâplanned for completion by Septemberâto eliminate road use. The school has also lobbied for a reduction in the speed limit from 60 mph to 40 mph, with advocacy ongoing for 30 mph. Coroner Dolan stated: 'I don't find sufficient evidence of gross failure. The school had a policy and took stepsâeven if implementation was flawed. William appeared inattentive when crossing, and there was opportunity to see the approaching vehicle.' Mrs. Avery-Wright said: 'We placed immense trust in the schoolâand those expectations were not met. We will continue our civil case.' In a post-inquest statement, Worth School apologized: 'We accept that the rule requiring escorting of Year 7 and 8 pupils across Paddockhurst Road was not enforced. For this failure, we apologize. We are committed to ensuring no other family endures this grief.' The school added that William remains in the prayers of the entire community.

article_content: (CNN) -- China's figure skating pair Shen Xue and Zhao Hongbo completed an emotional comeback at the Winter Olympics on Monday, capturing the gold medal in pairs figure skating. By winning, they earned China's first-ever Olympic gold in figure skating and fulfilled a long-standing dream that had previously eluded them. The husband-and-wife team had retired from competitive skating in 2007 but returned to the sport with the goal of securing Olympic gold. China secured a 1-2 finish in the event after Pan Qing and Tong Jian won silver, according to the Vancouver Olympics website. Germany's Aliona Savchenko and Robin Szolkowy took bronze. Elsewhere at the Games, South Korea's Mo Tae-Bum won gold in the men's 500-meter speed skating event. Japan's Keiichiro Nagashima and Joji Kato earned silver and bronze, respectively. Shen and Zhao had been among China's most decorated figure skaters, having won three world championships and two Olympic bronze medals before retiring. They married shortly after Zhao proposed to Shen on the ice following their 2007 World Championship victory in Tokyo. After headlining the U.S.-based Stars on Ice tour, retirement seemed a natural next step â but just two years later, they announced their return to compete in Vancouver, aiming for the gold that had always been out of reach. They kicked off their comeback by winning the Cup of China last season, then swept all three of their Grand Prix events and set a new world record at the Grand Prix Final. Ranked 29th in the world at the time of the Olympics and drawn to perform first among the 20 competing pairs â a position often considered disadvantageous â Shen and Zhao delivered a near-flawless short program on Sunday. Many analysts called it their strongest performance ever. 'We wanted the program to show everything we've accomplished, and we did it,' Zhao told Xinhua News Agency in Vancouver. 'It's the best Valentine's Day gift,' Shen added. CNN's Jo Ling Kent contributed to this report.

article_content: When Grant Wilson walks into a room, things donât always stay the same. Shadows move where no light falls. Whispers echo from empty corners. People report being shoved, grabbed, or thrown â all without anyone nearby. For Wilson, these arenât horror movie scenes; theyâre Tuesday afternoon. As co-host of the long-running Sci Fi Channel series 'Ghost Hunters,' he and his partner Jason Hawes have spent years investigating claims of hauntings across America. Their mission? To document the unexplained â and stay calm while doing it. 'Youâre going to get slapped, punched, pulled,' Wilson tells new recruits. 'Just expect it.' What started as a niche interest has exploded into a global obsession. Thanks to the showâs popularity, the group behind it â The Atlantic Paranormal Society (TAPS) â now has branches in over a dozen countries. Theyâve got a radio show, a magazine, T-shirts, live tours, and even fans who travel hundreds of miles just to attend a ghost hunt. 'Five years ago, talking about ghosts at work meant you were weird,' says David Schrader, host of 'Darkness Radio.' 'Now itâs dinner table conversation.' The trend didnât stop at TAPS. Networks rushed to copy the formula: 'Paranormal State,' 'Haunting Evidence,' 'A Haunting' â all trying to capture the same eerie magic. But behind the cameras, many investigators admit the real drama isnât in the EVP recordings or thermal readings. Itâs the rush to turn curiosity into content. 'Everyone I know has a pilot floating around,' Schrader laughs. 'Itâs like throwing Frisbees at a party.' For some, the drive comes from grief or loss â a longing to believe thereâs something after death. Others, like author Marley Gibson, say itâs about distraction. 'Weâre living through wars, economic hardship, broken healthcare systems,' she explains. 'People need a place to escape â even if itâs into a haunted attic.' The line between fear and fascination blurs. Investigators speak of sudden drops in temperature, unseen hands pressing against their backs, or hearing their child scream about a shadow in her room. One man, Patrick Burns, felt a massive finger â or maybe a paw â jab him in the lower back while working alone at home. The room froze. A loud thud shook the walls. He kept filming. 'I just said, Okay, youâve got my attention.' But Wilson says the scariest thing heâs ever encountered wasnât a spirit â it was a fan. At a public event, a woman approached him, lifted her pant leg, and revealed a tattoo of his face. 'She asked me what I thought,' he recalls. 'Thatâ¦ that creeped me out more than any ghost ever could.' And despite the adrenaline, most investigators insist theyâre not afraid. Just startled. And deeply respectful â many describe their work as rooted in faith, not fantasy. 'Iâve never met a more God-fearing group of people,' Gibson says. Whether theyâre blessing houses with holy water or chasing whispers in the dark, theyâre searching for meaning â not just monsters.

article_content: A trial against a Detroit police officer accused of fatally shooting a seven-year-old girl ended in a mistrial after the jury became hopelessly deadlocked. Jurors were unable to reach a verdict in the case against Officer Joseph Weekley, who was accused of shooting Aiyana Stanley-Jones during a police raid targeting a murder suspect in Detroit. Judge Cynthia Gray Hathaway declared a mistrial for the second time â the first having occurred in June 2013 after a similarly hung jury. On May 16, 2010, Aiyana Stanley-Jones, a happy-go-lucky seven-year-old, was shot and killed when a bullet from Weekleyâs submachine gun struck her in the head as she slept on a couch during a midnight raid. Police and the Special Response Team entered the home after throwing a stun grenade through a window. A camera crew from the TV show 'The First 48' was present outside but did not film the interior. During the trial, Weekleyâs defense argued that his weapon discharged accidentally during a physical struggle with Aiyanaâs grandmother, Mertilla Jones. She denied this account. Prosecutor Rob Moran emphasized that Weekleyâs training required him to keep his finger off the trigger, stating: 'All he had to do was follow his training â and we wouldnât be here.' The jury, composed of eight women and four men â including four African Americans â deliberated for four days, taking three votes and seeing some members change their positions. In the final vote, seven jurors voted not guilty, while five found Weekley guilty of the misdemeanor charge of careless, reckless, or negligent use of a firearm causing death. Jurors stated that race played no role in their deliberations, despite Weekley being white and Aiyana Black. The jury foreman, a pastor, described the case as deeply emotional: 'There were tears in this room.' Aiyanaâs mother, Dominika Stanley, and father, Charles Jones, sat in court sobbing after the announcement. Her great-uncle, Londell Fields, said: 'I don't understand how we can go through this again... and there not be a verdict either way.' Weekley released a statement before the mistrial, saying: 'I have already been devastated and my life has been ruined irreparably... I will be haunted by this tragedy for the rest of my life.' Fields responded: 'He should apologize and say he made a mistake.' Weekley could still face a third trial.

article_content: With millions of Indians glued to their screens during the ICC Cricket World Cup, smallcase manager Sonam Srivastava of Wright Research drew a clever parallel between cricket strategy and smart investing. Just as no cricket team can win relying only on batsmen or bowlers, your portfolio shouldnât depend solely on one asset class. A winning team needs all-rounders, specialist bowlers, solid batsmen, and sharp fielders â and your investments need the same balance. Think of equities as your all-rounder: they drive growth. Bonds? Theyâre your steady batsman, providing reliable returns even when things get shaky. Commodities act like bowlers â they help shield your portfolio from inflationâs heat. And real estate? Thatâs your fielder: tangible, grounding, and always in play. Imagine a team full of Virat Kohlis â brilliant in the chase, but useless when bowling. Or one made only of Mohammed Shami â lethal with the ball, but collapsing under pressure at the crease. Thatâs what happens when you put all your money in one basket. Diversification isnât optional; itâs essential. Tech has changed both cricket and finance. In cricket, LED bails and DRS made decisions fairer. In investing, platforms like smallcase let everyday investors access curated portfolios â much like how Team India used data analytics to outsmart opponents in the 2007 T20 World Cup. Markets shift like pitch conditions. One day itâs a dry, spinning track; the next, itâs a green seamer. The answer? Adapt. Stay invested. Use SIPs to smooth out volatility, just as Rahul Dravid did with his defensive mastery â he didnât just survive; he endured. A 97 from KL Rahul against Australia means more than a century against Afghanistan. Likewise, making money in a booming market is expected. But beating the odds during a crash? Thatâs true skill. Consistency, not flash, defines greatness â think Sachin Tendulkar, who played at the top for 24 years. Strong corporate governance and ESG practices? Theyâre the teamâs training regime. A disciplined board, ethical operations, and environmental responsibility donât just look good â they build trust, reduce risk, and fuel long-term value. Just like a well-drilled cricket squad, companies with strong foundations keep winning, even in tough conditions.

article_content: Last Monday, headlines screamed about an 'Internet Doomsday' â but the reality was far less catastrophic than feared. At the heart of the panic was the shutdown of emergency servers the FBI had kept running to keep millions of infected computers online. These machines had been compromised by a piece of malware called DNSChanger, which hijacked web traffic to redirect users to fake advertising sites â a scheme that netted cybercriminals $14 million. The FBI dismantled the criminalsâ infrastructure in late 2011, but instead of leaving users stranded, they set up temporary servers to give people time to clean up. On Monday, those safety nets were turned off. Around 211,000 devices worldwide â including just 42,000 in the U.S. â were still affected. Thatâs a dramatic drop from the 4 million machines infected at the peak. Experts credit public awareness campaigns led by Google, Facebook, and government agencies for helping users identify and fix their systems. If youâre unsure whether your device is compromised, visit dns-ok.us for a quick check. article_content: (CNN) â It would be easy to view the current conflict â with Hamas militants and smaller factions firing rockets into Israel, and Israel responding with heavy aerial bombardments â as a repeat of the 2008â2009 confrontation that killed more than 1,300 men, women, and children. But it is not. Hamas is now in a fundamentally different position. Still confined within Gazaâs densely populated neighborhoods, where it was elected six years ago, it now enjoys greater regional backing. What has changed stems from the Arab Spring, which dismantled some of Israelâs longtime regional allies and replaced them with leaders more sympathetic to Hamas. Israel and Hamas: How the conflict reignited. Gone is Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, whom Israel relied upon to enforce Gazaâs blockade and pressure Hamas during the 2008â2009 war. Gone too is the Egyptian stateâs prior suppression of free speech, which had dampened public anti-Israel sentiment. Instead â nearly unthinkable just four years ago â Hamasâs political leader held a live news conference in Cairo, even as Israeli airstrikes targeted Palestinian media outlets in Gaza. If proof of Egyptâs new stance was needed, this was it. Egypt didnât merely send Prime Minister Hisham Qandil to Gaza on Friday with expressions of solidarity; it also provided Hamas with a platform for propaganda at a critical moment. It is a dramatic reversal. Khalid Meshal, Hamasâs political chief, embraced the spotlight, praising Egyptâs newly supportive posture. Q&A: What is Hamas? But Egypt is far from the only actor reshaping the region to Israelâs disadvantage. The small Gulf state of Qatar has emerged as one of the most influential political players, actively shaping regional dynamics. Qatar has backed governments like Egyptâs, which have ties to the moderate Islamist Muslim Brotherhood â of which Hamas, though a radical offshoot, has long maintained ideological links. Last month, during a historic visit to Gaza, the Emir of Qatar pledged $400 million in aid, signaling an effort to draw Hamas away from Iran and closer to Doha. Qatar has been cultivating this relationship for years. When Hamas leader Khalid Meshal fled Syria amid its escalating civil war earlier this year, it was Qatar that offered him safe haven. Today, Qatar wields leverage it previously lacked. So where does this leave Israel? Simply put: while Israel remains militarily superior, it is diplomatically weaker than it was in 2009. Why Israel might hesitate to launch a ground invasion. Egypt is no longer willing to enforce the blockade at the Rafah border crossing or provide the level of intelligence cooperation it once did. In fact, some estimates suggest Egyptâs security services no longer fully control Islamist militant networks, many of whom have been released from prison and are quietly regrouping in Cairoâs sprawling suburbs or the lawless Sinai Peninsula, which borders Israel. If the Israeli government hoped to rely on remnants of Mubarak-era cooperation, it will be disappointed. Todayâs Egyptian rhetoric, while stopping short of formally abandoning its peace treaty with Israel, has clearly adopted a pro-Hamas tone. Across the Arab world, widespread public disapproval of Israelâs policies toward Palestinians has long been a constant. In the past, most Arab leaders were autocrats who could ignore popular sentiment. No longer. The regionâs new, democratically elected leaders are acutely aware of the hardline opposition waiting to exploit any perceived betrayal of Palestinian rights. Smuggling weapons to Gaza â the long way.

article_content: In 2002, when she was just three months old, Charlotte Ponce of Spring Lake, Michigan, suffered a devastating raccoon attack that destroyed her right ear, nose, and part of her lip. Left unsupervised while her teenage parents were away, Charlotte was severely injured after the animal escaped its cage. Her great-aunt Sharon and great-uncle Tim took custody of Charlotte and her younger brother Marshall, dedicating their lives to her care. They raised over $10,000 to fund her ongoing medical treatments, and Sharon left her job to become Charlotteâs full-time caregiver. In 2012, Dr. Kongrit Chaiyasate of Beaumont Hospital in Royal Oak, Michigan, successfully reconstructed Charlotteâs nose. Now, at age 12, she has undergone another pioneering procedure: the implantation of rib cartilage into her forearm, where it will grow into the shape of a natural ear over the coming months. Scheduled for June, the next surgery will transplant the grown cartilage onto her headâa highly complex operation considered extremely rare in medical history. Dr. Chaiyasate, aware of the precision required, practiced the delicate carving technique on potatoes to perfect his approach. Although Charlotte once wore a prosthetic ear, it caused repeated infections and discomfort. The new biological ear offers a permanent, functional, and natural solution. article_content: Gaza City â The four boys were cousins, playing as they often had on the sunlit shore of the Mediterranean when the shelling began. A first shell hit a fishermanâs hut on the jetty beside them. As smoke rose, some ran for coverâbut they couldnât escape the second explosion. The attack killed Ismail, Zakaria, Ahed, and Mohamed, all between the ages of 9 and 11, from the extended Bakr family. The Israeli military said it is investigating the strike and believes the target was Hamas operatives, calling the deaths of the children a 'tragic outcome.' Yet children have repeatedly borne the brunt of this conflict: over 200 people have died in 10 days of Israeli bombardment, nearly 40 of them children, according to the United Nations. Journalists stationed in a nearby hotel witnessed the horror. Nicholas Casey of the Wall Street Journal described seeing a boy, about 9 or 10, with severe burns and a twisted leg. NBCâs Ayman Mohyeldin recalled kicking a ball with the boys just minutes before they died. Their parents had warned them not to go outside due to frequent airstrikes. But the urge to play under the sun proved too strong. 'Why did he go to the beachâto have them take him from me?' sobbed Mohamedâs mother. While Israeli families near Gaza scramble to bomb shelters, fearing rocket fire, Palestinians in Gaza have no such refuge. Many say warningsâleaflets, phone calls, nonlethal strikesâare insufficient. 'Were those four small boys firing rockets?' asked Sufian, a relative. 'They went to play football.' Ramiz, Mohamedâs blind father, said, 'I felt the world had ended.' The boys were buried within an hour. Hundreds attended the funeral, chanting anger into the air. Human rights groups question whether Israelâs precautions are enough. The Israeli military insists it avoids civilian harmâbut for families like the Bakrs, the cost is unbearable.

article_content: A professional baseball player was hospitalized this week after suffering a bite wound to the ear during a minor league game. Alex Guerrero, a second baseman for the Albuquerque Isotopes, was involved in a heated altercation with teammate Miguel Olivo during a match against the Salt Lake Bees on Tuesday. Video footage from MiLB.com, the official site of Minor League Baseball, shows teammates intervening as the two exchanged taunts on the field. Later, in the eighth inning, the conflict escalated inside the teamâs dugout. Photos show Guerrero holding a towel to his ear. The game was briefly suspended, and both players were removed from the lineup. Guerrero was transported to a hospital in Murray, Utah. According to Salt Lake Police Detective Greg Wilking, authorities were informed that 'an ear had been bitten off' â though no official medical confirmation has been released. Guerrero declined to file a formal police report, stating he wished to consult with a lawyer and Major League Baseball before deciding on next steps. The Isotopes lost the game 7â4, having allowed four runs in the first inning. Olivo reportedly became upset after Guerrero failed to tag out a runner following a throw from him in the seventh inning. The Los Angeles Dodgers, the Isotopesâ Triple-A affiliate, issued a statement condemning the behavior: 'The baseball operations department is aware of the altercation and is conducting an investigation into the matter. article_content: In Qatar, two university students have engineered a groundbreaking 3D printer capable of producing real, edible vegetables â starting with carrots â using lab-grown plant cells and ultraviolet light. Mohammad Annan, 20, and Lujain Al Mansoori, 21, both studying information systems at Carnegie Mellon University in Doha, designed the entire machine themselves after sourcing components globally. Their invention, which won top honors in the FoodTech category at a recent hackathon hosted by Qatar Development Bank, represents a leap beyond earlier 3D food printers that relied on mashed fruits and vegetables. Unlike those methods, which are slow and unsuitable for large-scale use, their system mimics industrial masked stereolithography, curing edible 'ink' made from cultivated plant cells with UV light to rapidly form solid shapes. The result? A carrot that matches the nutritional profile of one grown in soil, but without needing farmland. With only 2.5% of Qatarâs territory suitable for farming, the duo sees their tech as a way to cut heavy import dependence. They chose carrots first because theyâre well-studied in plant biology, but their goal is to print rare, climate-vulnerable crops like certain fruits and vegetables that struggle to grow in changing environments. Al Mansoori notes that while early versions of 3D food tech were aimed at helping people with chewing difficulties, theirs is built for volume â and affordability. Currently, three kilograms of their printed carrots cost 10 QAR ($2.75), less than traditional ones. They envision a future where these printers sit in supermarkets, hospitals, and even homes, helping feed populations worldwide â especially where land scarcity, conflict, or climate disruption threaten food access.

article_content: On the final day of the summer transfer window, Manchester City stunned the football world by securing Brazilian star Robinho from Real Madrid for a record-breaking Â£32.5 million â a deal made possible only after the clubâs dramatic takeover by Abu Dhabiâs United Group. While Chelsea had been heavily favored to land the 24-year-old forward, Real Madrid held firm against multiple bids, waiting for a buyer willing to match their valuation. Enter City, flush with new Middle Eastern cash, who pulled off the coup no one expected. Robinho, who had publicly expressed interest in joining Chelsea, ultimately chose City â citing the presence of fellow Brazilians Jo and Elano, and his confidence in manager Mark Hughesâ long-term vision. 'I saw the ambition here,' Robinho told Cityâs official website. 'This isnât just another club â itâs a project I want to be part of.' He also praised Hughes, noting the former Barcelona playerâs experience would be invaluable in helping him grow at the highest level. City didnât stop there. They nearly stole Tottenhamâs Dimitar Berbatov away from Manchester United, submitting a bid that was accepted by Spurs â only for the Bulgarian striker to choose United at the last minute. 'It was very close,' admitted Sulaiman Al-Fahim, a key figure in the Abu Dhabi deal. 'We were unlucky.' The clubâs new ownership marks a seismic shift. Thaksin Shinawatra, whose brief tenure ended amid corruption allegations and asset freezes in Thailand, has stepped aside â retaining only a minor stake and the ceremonial title of honorary president. The Abu Dhabi group, led by investors including Al-Fahim and representatives from the Emirates Group, now controls all operational decisions. Their goal? Top-four finish, Champions League football, and turning City into a global powerhouse. With City sitting third in the Premier League after three games, and Hughes set to receive full backing for future signings, the message is clear: this is only the beginning.

article_content: According to a European Parliament report, hundreds of millions of euros in EU disaster aid intended for victims of the 2009 LâAquila earthquake may have been diverted to companies linked to organized crime. Despite requirements that subcontractors obtain Mafia-free certification, a draft report by Danish MEP Soren Bo Sondergaard revealed serious allegations that funds were paid to firms with direct or indirect ties to organized crime. Investigators found wanted criminals operating from buildings reconstructed with EU money. The report also condemned the use of substandard, flammable, and hazardous construction materials, labeling the work as dangerous and poorly executed. article_content: The gunman who took three people hostage at the Discovery Channel headquarters in Silver Spring, Maryland, was once convicted of smuggling an undocumented immigrant into the United States from Mexico. This history stands in sharp contrast to the manifesto he left behind â a document condemning immigration, farming, automotive pollution, and what he called 'the whole blasted human economy.' On immigration, the manifesto demanded: 'Programs must be developed to find solutions to stopping ALL immigration pollution and the anchor baby filth that follows that. Find solutions to stopping it.' Lee was killed by police on Wednesday after a hours-long standoff. The three hostages were unharmed. Authorities confirmed that Lee used two starter pistols during the incident â not handguns, as initially reported. article_content: The brutal murder of a British soldier on a London street in June 2013 has reignited fears about the growing threat of 'open-source jihad' â a form of terrorism where lone actors, radicalized online, strike with minimal planning and no direct organizational ties. 'Itâs always the one we feared,' said former London police chief John Yates. 'The lone wolf who appears from nowhere, unseen by intelligence agencies.' On June 5, 2013, two men attacked the soldier near his barracks in Woolwich, southeast London, using cleavers. They recorded a video declaring, 'We swear by Almighty Allah we will never stop fighting you until you leave us alone... this British soldier is an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth.' Their rhetoric echoed classic al Qaeda messaging. Experts trace this shift to Abu Musab al-Suri, a radical thinker who, after al Qaeda lost its Afghan base, proposed a new model: 'Every Muslim should be an army of one.' This decentralized approach was operationalized by al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP) through the online sermons of Anwar al-Awlaki â killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2011 â and the publication of 'Inspire,' an English-language magazine offering step-by-step guidance for low-tech attacks. 'Think small, think easy, think unsophisticated,' AQAP instructed followers. 'Donât attempt 9/11-style plots â theyâre too hard to hide. Just buy a knife, find a symbolic target, and strike.' Such attacks are nearly impossible to prevent because they require no funding, training, or coordination. Cases like Roshonara Choudhry â a British student who stabbed MP Stephen Timms in 2010 after watching al-Awlakiâs videos â and the Boston Marathon bombers, who used a pressure-cooker design from 'Inspire,' demonstrate the real-world impact of this strategy. Even those with no prior criminal history can become dangerous. John Yates noted that Choudhry had never been flagged by authorities. 'You canât surveil everyone,' he said. 'We need better community engagement â because communities defeat terrorism.' In response, the UK government has revived proposals to expand internet surveillance powers, including monitoring downloads of extremist content like 'Inspire.' Critics warn such measures risk infringing on free speech and privacy. Yet, as Maher argues, 'You donât even need to download 'Inspire' anymore â the idea is everywhere, amplified by media coverage.' The challenge isnât just technological â itâs ideological. Preventing lone-wolf attacks requires not just more surveillance, but deeper trust between security services and vulnerable communities.

article_content: A 29-year-old Australian weightlifter, widely believed to be Francois Etoundi, was taken into custody early Wednesday morning following an alleged assault at the Commonwealth Games athletesâ village in Glasgow. Adding to the chaos, Papua New Guinean weightlifter Toua Udia, 22, was arrested on suspicion of sexual assault at a nearby Tesco supermarket. article_content: Johannesburg, South Africa (CNN) â In the wake of Nelson Mandelaâs passing at age 95, family representatives expressed heartfelt gratitude for the overwhelming wave of global support. General Themba Matanzima, speaking on behalf of the Mandela family, described the former president as 'the pillar of the family,' adding, 'But in our hearts and souls, he will always be with us.' Matanzima highlighted Mandelaâs enduring values â humility, compassion, and an unwavering belief in education as a tool to lift children out of poverty. 'A life lived for others is a life well-lived,' he said, echoing Mandelaâs personal philosophy. Despite achieving global iconic status, Matanzima noted, Mandela remained deeply grounded within his family. He stressed that the family would honor his legacy by continuing to champion the principles he lived â and died â for. Tributes are being planned across South Africa. A state funeral will take place on December 15 in Qunu, Eastern Cape. On Sunday, the nation will observe a day of prayer and reflection. An official memorial service will be held Tuesday at Johannesburgâs First National Bank Stadium, with world leaders, including U.S. President Barack Obama, expected to attend. Mandelaâs body will lie in state in Pretoria from Wednesday until next Friday. President Jacob Zuma, who announced Mandelaâs death in a televised address, called him 'our nationâs greatest son' and 'a father to our people.' Flags across South Africa are flying at half-staff until the funeral. The United States and the UKâs Buckingham Palace have also lowered their flags in tribute. Mandelaâs journey â from anti-apartheid activist to political prisoner to president â remains one of historyâs most powerful stories of resilience and reconciliation. 'When I walked out of prison,' he once said, 'I knew that if I didnât leave my bitterness behind, Iâd still be imprisoned.' Four years after his release, he became South Africaâs first Black president, uniting a fractured nation through forgiveness. In his later years, Mandela endured repeated hospitalizations due to a chronic lung condition. Yet even then, his spirit remained a beacon. As President Obama remarked, 'He no longer belongs to us â he belongs to the ages.'

article_content: A group identifying itself as Saudi Arabian hackers has posted the credit card details and personal information of thousands of Israelis online, triggering an international investigation. On Tuesday, the group â calling itself 'group-xp' and led by 'OxOmar' â claimed to have released 400,000 credit card numbers in a message posted on a hacked Israeli sports website. 'We are anonymous Saudi Arabian hackers. We decided to release the first part of our data about Israel,' the post read. However, the Bank of Israel countered that, according to credit card issuers, only around 15,000 cards were affected â all of which have since been blocked from online and phone transactions. On Thursday, the group claimed to have released an additional 11,000 card numbers and threatened further leaks. Yoram Hacohen, head of Israelâs Law, Information and Technology Authority, told CNN that while the credit card data is concerning, the real danger lies in the exposure of private information: email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, and passwords â all of which can enable identity theft. Hacohen stressed that because some of the exposed data belongs to Jews globally â not only Israelis â this constitutes a crime against citizens worldwide. Israeli authorities have launched a criminal investigation, including a digital forensic probe, to trace the attackers. Under Israelâs Privacy Protection Law, such theft is illegal. Yet tracking cybercriminals remains extremely difficult. Officials are now appealing for international assistance. Israeli columnist Ben Caspit, writing in Maariv, suggested the incident might be a prank, a youth stunt, a beginner-level hate attack, or even a covert operation linked to Iranian intelligence. This comes amid heightened awareness of cyber threats in Israel. In May 2011, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu established the National Cyber Headquarters to safeguard critical infrastructure â including power grids, communications, banking, water systems, and transportation. In December, he noted that this cyber defense unit, alongside missile shields and physical barriers, is essential to protecting the nation from its adversaries. An official confirmed the agency is still being established.

article_content: Once housing nuclear missiles, a 50-foot Cold War-era missile silo has been transformed into a luxury residence by developers Bruce James Franscio and Gregory Gibbons and is now on the market for Â£2 million. Located in the picturesque Adirondack State Park near Lake Placid â host of the 1980 Winter Olympics â the property appears at ground level as a modest log cabin, but conceals a vast underground complex beneath. The reinforced silo, originally designed to withstand a direct nuclear strike, now features a two-level home with three bedrooms, two bathrooms, an open-plan living area, and a kitchen with granite countertops. Access to the underground launch control center requires entering a code through a heavy metal door in the kitchen, leading down a 50-foot tunnel to the former missile storage chamber. Franscio, a former pilot, purchased the derelict silo with Gibbons in the early 1990s after it had been exposed to groundwater for three decades. Extensive renovation restored its structural integrity while adapting it for modern living. The property also includes a private jet runway and hangar, adding to its exclusivity. Franscio says the home is ideal not only as a unique residence but also for yoga retreats, corporate events, or as a community hub, given the parkâs abundance of outdoor activities like hiking and cycling. article_content: Karen Johnson Swift, a 44-year-old mother of four from Dyersburg, Tennessee, has been missing since October 30, after her husband reported her disappearance. Her carâa white 2004 Nissan Muranoâwas found abandoned with a flat tire approximately a quarter-mile from her home. Nearby, in some bushes, investigators discovered a pair of jeans and a gray zip-up top, which a friend confirmed belonged to her. DNA samples from her mother were matched to the clothing, though police await final confirmation from the state crime lab. Swift was last seen on Halloween morning after returning from dropping off her children following a sleepover. When her youngest daughter awoke at 6 a.m., her mother was gone. The child has since become withdrawn, barely eating, according to family members. Although the couple had filed for divorce on October 11, they continued living together. David Swift, her husband, told police he last saw her at home. He has since retained legal counsel and ceased communication with investigators. Authorities have not named him a person of interest. A neighbor, 39-year-old John Hogshooter, was arrested in early October for allegedly poisoning two dogsâone belonging to the Swift family. Reports indicate Swift had attempted to confront him about the incident shortly before vanishing, but he was not home. Law enforcement has not linked him to her disappearance. Her cellphone, last used at 5 a.m. on Halloween to access the internet, is missing. Police are working with her carrier to determine its last known location. No signs of foul play have been confirmed, and the case remains classified as a missing persons investigation. Friends and community members describe Swift as deeply devoted to her children and unlikely to leave voluntarily. Vigils are being held in downtown Dyersburg, and aerial searches have been deployed across rural areas. Authorities continue reviewing all evidence, including potential connections to the unsolved 2011 abduction of 21-year-old nursing student Holly Boboâlocated just 80 miles awayâbut no official link has been established.

article_content: An infestation of large, green-fanged tube web spiders (Segestria florentina) has alarmed a family in Southampton. Dan Jackson, 29, and his three-year-old son Ruben are uneasy about spending time outdoors, as the spiders have colonized gaps and crevices in their garden and exterior walls. These black spiders, identifiable by their glossy green fangs, construct distinctive tube-shaped webs in cracks and lie in wait for preyâsuch as cockroaches, moths, bees, and waspsâto brush against their silk threads. Mr. Jackson is concerned the spiders may enter the house and bite his young son. While their bite delivers a sharp, injection-like pain that can last for hours, their venom causes no lasting health effects. Originally from the Mediterranean, Segestria florentina has been established in Britain for nearly a century and is most commonly seen between June and November. Females grow up to 22mm in body length; males up to 15mm. Jackson first noticed one spider in his garden but was startled when dozens emerged at dusk. 'Iâm not scared of spiders,' he said, 'but even Iâm freaked out by these. I saw one the size of a tablespoonâit shot off the ground like a bolt when I tried to observe it.' Though sometimes mistaken for the deadly Australian funnel-web spider due to similar hunting behavior, Segestria florentina poses no serious threat to humans. Jackson is now considering contacting local authorities or a pest control service to address the situation.

article_content: Sir Paul McCartney's childhood home in Liverpool sold at auction in just six minutes to an anonymous local buyer for Â£150,000. By contrast, Ringo Starrâs childhood home on Madryn Street â once valued at Â£60,000 in 2013 â is now worth just Â£525. article_content: By Jack Doyle. PUBLISHED: 18:35 EST, 27 March 2012. | UPDATED: 03:34 EST, 28 March 2012. Radical preacher: Unlike Italy, Britain has delayed deporting Abu Qatada (above) due to a ruling by the European Court of Human Rights blocking the move. For years, successive UK governments have maintained that extremist preacher Abu Qatada cannot be deported, arguing it would violate his human rights. Perhaps Britain should consider Italyâs approach. Yesterday, the European Court of Human Rights acknowledged its limited ability to enforce its rulings in the case of Mohamed Mannai, a convicted terrorist deported from Italy to Tunisia in 2010. Although the Strasbourg court ordered Italy to compensate Mannai for violating its interim injunction, officials confirmed they cannot compel Italy to return him, as Tunisia lies outside the ECHRâs jurisdiction. A spokesperson stated: 'Once the applicant has been deported, there is little we can doâhe is in Tunisia, a country outside the jurisdiction of the European Court of Human Rights.' Last night, the ruling reignited calls for UK ministers to emulate Italyâs actions and deport Qatada. The UK government contends that radical Islamist Abu Qatadaâdescribed by a judge as Osama bin Ladenâs right-hand man in Europeâcannot be sent to Jordan because an ECHR ruling determined he would not receive a fair trial there, given the high probability that evidence obtained through torture would be used. Conservative MP Dominic Raab, representing Esher and Walton, said: 'The Italian and French governments have a track record of disregarding Strasbourg in deportation cases involving torture risksâwith minimal consequences. In the Qatada case, Strasbourg exceeded the bounds of existing human rights law. Having gone to great lengths to accommodate this questionable ruling, we must now put him on a flight to Jordan without delay.' Mannai was sentenced in October 2006 to five years and four months after being convicted alongside two others linked to the radical group Ansar al-Islam on terrorism charges. Police said the cell planned attacks in Italy and radicalized recruits to act as suicide bombers. Following his conviction, a Milan court ordered Mannaiâs deportation upon release. However, the ECHR issued an interim order suspending the deportation pending review. Despite this, Mannai was flown back to Tunisia within months of completing his sentence in February 2010. Yesterday, the ECHR condemned Italy for ignoring its ruling and ordered it to pay Mannai â¬15,000 (Â£12,500) plus legal expenses. The Council of Europe also expressed deep concern over Italyâs actions. Italy had previously defied a similar ECHR ruling in June 2008 when it deported convicted terrorist Ben Khemais to Tunisia. Home Secretary Theresa May is currently negotiating with Jordan for legally binding assurances that Qatada would receive a fair trial. In a recent interview, May refused five times to confirm whether she would defy the ECHRâs ruling. However, she emphasized that her objective is to establish a lawful path to deport Qatada so the government is no longer compelled by any court to retain him. A Whitehall official noted that Mannai was deported while his case was still under review, whereas a final ECHR judgment has already been issued regarding Qatada. Government lawyers warn that attempting to deport him now would constitute contempt of court.

article_content: A recent study involving 61 Australian men has revealed that treating sleep apnoea with CPAP therapy can significantly enhance sexual well-being â even more so than relying solely on erectile dysfunction medications. Conducted between 2010 and 2013 by researchers at Sydneyâs Royal Prince Alfred Hospital, the study focused on men experiencing both obstructive sleep apnoea and difficulty achieving or maintaining erections. Participants were divided into four groups: some received CPAP machines to keep airways open during sleep, others were given placebos, a third group took ED drugs like sildenafil, and a fourth received no treatment. Over three months, scientists tracked not only self-reported sexual satisfaction but also monitored nighttime erections using sleep lab technology. They discovered that men using CPAP experienced a marked increase in nocturnal erections â natural physiological events that typically occur every 90 minutes during REM sleep. Dr. Kerri Melehan, lead researcher, explained that sleep apnoea fragments REM cycles, depriving the body of these essential âpracticeâ periods for erectile function. As a result, consistent CPAP use restored normal patterns, leading to higher overall sexual satisfaction. While ED medications helped some men, CPAP offered broader benefits by addressing the root cause: disrupted sleep. Dr. Melehan emphasized that treating the underlying sleep disorder can be more effective long-term than symptom-focused pills. These findings are set to be unveiled at the 26th Australasian Sleep Conference in Perth, aiming to encourage men to prioritize sleep health as a cornerstone of sexual and overall wellness.

article_content: CNN â This week, the concept of learning through play reached a new level. The LEGO Foundation, the charitable arm of the LEGO Group, has opened a school in Billund, Denmark, designed to offer young children a creative, play-centered approach to education. The school was conceived by billionaire Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen, who led the LEGO Group for over two decades and is the grandson of LEGOâs founder, Ole Kirk Kristiansen. The International School of Billund welcomed approximately 75 students, aged three to seven, on its first day of classes. The institution delivers the traditional curriculum mandated by the Danish government while integrating play-based pedagogy. Located in the same town as LEGOâs global headquarters, the school aims to become a model for innovative early childhood education. Camilla Uhre Fog, a director at the LEGO Foundation and chair of the schoolâs board, said the school plans to invite LEGO employees to visit and teach students. Classes may also serve as a testing ground for new educational products and innovations. 'We want to be a role model,' she said. 'Everyone has something they can give back to children.' The LEGO Foundation intends to collaborate with the school to deepen understanding of child development and product designâbut 'we will never compromise on education or the childâs development,' Uhre Fog emphasized. Paul Hansford enrolled his son Lukas in the schoolâs kindergarten program this year. He praised its focus on inquiry-based learning and English language development. 'Everything weâve heard about it seems very positive,' he said after the first day. The LEGO Foundation owns 25% of the LEGO Group and supports global research and educational initiatives. In 2012, the LEGO Foundation, LEGO Charity, and related family foundations donated approximately 148 million Danish kroner ($26.5 million) to charitable causes. article_content: (CNN) â A fire at a refinery in Washington state killed four people and injured three, a spokeswoman for Harborview Medical Center said Friday. Tesoro Corp., the company that owns the refinery, initially reported three fatalities. A fourth victim â a 29-year-old woman â later died from her injuries at Harborview Medical Center in Seattle, according to medical center spokeswoman Susan Gregg-Hanson. Three others â a 36-year-old woman, a 34-year-old man, and a 41-year-old man â remain in critical condition with severe burns, Gregg-Hanson added. None of the deceased have been publicly identified. The fire erupted shortly after midnight at the naphtha unit of the Anacortes, Washington, refinery during maintenance operations, according to Tesoro. It was contained by approximately 2 a.m. Friday, and affected units have been shut down, the company stated on its website. CNN affiliate KCPQ reported that three workers were initially listed as missing, and a search was underway. The cause of the fire remains under investigation. Residents reported feeling an explosion up to five miles away. "This is a very sad time for our organization," said Bruce Smith, Tesoroâs chairman, president, and CEO. "Everyone in the Tesoro family recognizes the profound impact this tragedy will have on the families involved, and we are acting swiftly to ensure the safety of our employees, contractors, and the surrounding community." Tesoro has not yet responded to additional media inquiries. Tesoro Corp. is an independent refiner and marketer of petroleum products. Through its subsidiaries, it operates seven refineries across the western United States with a combined capacity of approximately 665,000 barrels per day. Anacortes is located about 80 miles south of Vancouver, British Columbia.

article_content: Over the last twelve months, Iâve returned to several Southeast Asian nations I first explored more than ten years ago â and what I saw surprised me. This isnât just growth; itâs transformation. Economies once overlooked are now drawing global attention as investors shift away from Chinaâs cooling market and rising labor costs. At the heart of this change is ASEAN â a loose alliance of ten countries thatâs quietly becoming one of the worldâs most dynamic economic engines. In Vientiane, I met a couple â one from Malaysia, the other from Laos â who met during academic exchanges in Japan. After earning their degrees, they chose to return home not to isolate themselves, but to serve their region. Their story mirrors a new generation of Southeast Asians who see their futures tied not to narrow national borders, but to a shared regional identity. While the world watches Beijingâs âChina Dream,â a quieter but equally powerful vision is taking shape: the ASEAN Dream. Unlike the EU, ASEAN doesnât have a unified currency or parliament â yet itâs outpacing Europe in momentum. Despite centuries of rivalry and conflict, member states are deepening trade, investing across borders, and growing at over 5% annually â even as traditional markets like Europe stall. With 600 million people and a projected GDP of nearly $5 trillion by 2020, ASEAN is already wealthier than India in economic output despite having fewer citizens. Its location is no accident: it sits squarely between China and India, and the Strait of Malacca â the worldâs busiest shipping lane â runs right through it. Oil, electronics, and goods flow here daily, making ASEAN indispensable to global supply chains. But growth alone isnât enough. Decades of colonial rule, war, dictatorship, and isolation have left deep scars. Today, the region is mostly peaceful â except for tensions over the South China Sea and Chinaâs construction of upstream dams on the Mekong River, threatening water supplies for millions in Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam. To thrive, ASEAN must go beyond trade deals. Infrastructure is the missing link. Only Singapore has fully developed first-world infrastructure. Vietnam and Malaysia have made strong progress, while Indonesia, Thailand, and the Philippines are now accelerating road, rail, and port projects â finally prioritizing long-term investment after years of neglect. And itâs not just concrete and steel. Real progress means lifting up the rural poor in Myanmar and Cambodia with better schools, clinics, and farming tools. It means preparing millions of young people entering cities for jobs in healthcare, tech, and logistics â not just slums and traffic jams. For too long, ASEAN was seen as a talking shop. Now, it has the chance to become the central hub connecting Asiaâs giants â a network of smart cities, shared prosperity, and stable governance. The next decade wonât just decide its economy â it will define whether this region becomes a model for the 21st century.

article_content: Los Angeles, California (CNN) â Prosecutors announced Friday that charges related to Michael Jacksonâs death will be filed on Monday, though they did not specify the nature of the charges or the individual to be charged. Dr. Conrad Murray, Jacksonâs personal physician at the time of his death in June 2009, had planned to surrender to authorities at a Los Angeles courthouse branch near LAX on Friday afternoon. However, prosecutors delayed filing charges, prompting Murray and his attorney, Ed Chernoff, to cancel their planned public appearance near the courthouse. In a written statement, Chernoff said media access would remain closed until after Murrayâs arraignment, citing the district attorneyâs announcement. Negotiations between Murrayâs legal team and prosecutors on Thursday to arrange a voluntary surrender had reportedly broken down, according to a law enforcement source familiar with the talks. Chernoff emphasized that his client had consistently offered to surrender at any time and location designated by law enforcement, arguing that a public arrest would be an unnecessary use of resources. 'Weâve always made it clear: You tell us where; weâll be there,' he said. Murray, who traveled from Houston to Los Angeles last week anticipating charges, was hired in spring 2009 to support Jacksonâs preparation for his upcoming London concert series. According to a police affidavit, Murray administered nightly IV infusions of propofol â a powerful anesthetic â to help Jackson sleep, despite concerns about dependency. On the morning of June 25, Murray reported leaving Jacksonâs bedroom for no more than two minutes. Upon returning, he found Jackson unresponsive. He remained with him as emergency crews transported Jackson to UCLA Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead at 2:26 p.m. The Los Angeles County coroner later ruled Jacksonâs death a homicide caused by acute propofol intoxication, with additional contributing factors including the effects of benzodiazepines such as lorazepam. Murray told investigators he had given Jackson three benzodiazepines in the hours before his death and had attempted to taper him off propofol over the prior six weeks of treatment.

article_content: Detectives are investigating the discovery of human remains hidden in the foundations of a pizzeria in Lecco, Italy, recently seized as part of an anti-Mafia operation. The grim find was made during renovation work at the building, which sits atop an ancient Roman road and dates back to the 1600s. Forensic experts believe the bones are from a much more recent period. The pizzeria, known as Il Giglio, was confiscated following investigations into the Coco Trovato clan, a faction of the 'Ndrangheta â the powerful Calabrian organized crime network based in southern Italy. Officers and forensic pathologists were called to the site after workers uncovered the remains, just days after ornate frescoes were discovered in the same building. Experts from Italyâs Superintendency of Art had been scheduled to assess the artwork, but their work has been paused since the property was transferred to local police control. Plans to convert the site into a senior care facility have been put on hold. Franco Coco Trovato, the clanâs former leader, was sentenced to life in prison in 1992 for murder, extortion, and drug trafficking. Even from behind bars, authorities believe he continues to exert influence over the group. The 'Ndrangheta has significantly expanded its operations into northern Italy, particularly Milan, where it dominates the cocaine trade. Investigators estimate the syndicate earns over Â£30 billion annually â comparable to Sloveniaâs GDP. The group is also linked to the 2007 Duisburg massacre in Germany, where six members were killed in a pizzeria during a violent feud. Due to the organizationâs tight-knit family structure and low rate of informants, law enforcement struggles to dismantle its networks. Authorities suspect the 'Ndrangheta has connections in the UK and other parts of Europe.

article_content: Last night, intimate details of a four-year romantic relationship between British MP Mike Hancock and his young Russian researcher, Ekaterina Zatuliveter, were made public â just as she was cleared of allegations that she was a Russian spy. At just 21 years old, Zatuliveter wrote in her diary about her deep affection for Hancock, whom she affectionately called 'my darling Teddy Bear' and 'King Louis' â a playful nod to Disneyâs The Jungle Book. Her writings, filled with teenage-like longing, described her desire to feel him 'with all my naked body' and expressed anxiety over his whereabouts during his travels. These personal entries became central to her successful appeal against deportation. The Special Immigration Appeals Commission (SIAC) called the diary 'compelling evidence' that the relationship was sincere and not part of a coordinated espionage plot, as claimed by MI5. Despite Hancock being 40 years her senior and married for over four decades, the tribunal concluded: 'However odd it might seem, she fell for him.' Zatuliveter, now 26, admitted she was stunned by the verdict. She accused UK security agencies of being 'unprofessional and paranoid,' comparing her ordeal to 'a person on horseback with a sword facing tanks and aircraft.' To prove she wasnât a spy, she said she had no choice but to expose deeply private aspects of her life to the public. The diary, which surfaced during the tribunal despite her earlier denial of keeping one, covered the period from 2004 to 2007. It revealed not only her romance with Hancock but also her conflicted feelings about older men â even listing four men she considered potential 'victims.' The panel described her as an 'immature, calculating, emotional and self-centred young woman.' One entry, in which she believed Hancock was in Iraq, turned out to be false â he was actually in Paris. The tribunal suggested this might have been a fabrication by Zatuliveter, but ultimately concluded Hancock had misled her. While the court found no credible evidence she was a Russian agent, officials stood by their initial suspicions, leaving open the possibility that she was a 'supremely competent and rigorously trained operative' who fooled them all. The Home Office expressed disappointment, noting the court acknowledged 'ample grounds for suspicion' â yet still ruled in her favor. For Zatuliveter, the victory came at a steep personal cost: her privacy, dignity, and peace of mind.

article_content: A retired prosecutor, David Wells, has publicly admitted to lying about his involvement in the 1978 Roman Polanski sex case, as depicted in the 2008 HBO documentary 'Roman Polanski: Wanted and Desired.' In the film, Wells claimed he pressured Judge Laurence Rittenband to imprison Polanski, even alleging he showed the judge a photo of the director smirking with two womenâinterpreting it as a gesture of defiance. He also said he urged a 90-day diagnostic evaluation at Chino prison. Now, Wells confesses to fabricating all of these claims. He told CNNâs Wolf Blitzer that he exaggerated his role to make himself seem more significant and to 'liven up' the documentary. He never held private discussions with the judge about sentencing, nor did he personally hand the photo to Rittenbandâhe passed it along through court staff. His false statements had serious consequences: they fueled accusations of judicial misconduct and gave Polanski renewed grounds to seek dismissal of the decades-old case. But Polanskiâs refusal to return to the U.S. stalled those efforts. Wells also admitted lying to The New York Times in 2008, saying he feared being exposed as a minor figure in a high-profile case. He added that he never imagined the documentary would air widely in America. The documentaryâs director, Marina Zenovich, expressed shock and sadness, noting Wells had signed consent forms and publicly endorsed the filmâs accuracy at the time. Wells has agreed to undergo a polygraph test to corroborate his recantation, pending approval from his former employerâthe Los Angeles County District Attorneyâs Officeâwhich has no jurisdiction over him since his retirement. Polanski, who pleaded guilty to unlawful sexual intercourse with a 13-year-old girl in exchange for a sentence that included time served and probation, fled the U.S. in 1978 after learning the judge might renege on the deal. He was arrested in Switzerland in 2009 and is fighting extradition. Wells, once a low-level calendar prosecutor, now says he regretted inflating his role. 'When you peel away all the feathers, it's just a lie,' he said. 'I shouldnât have done it. I wish I didnât.'

article_content: An Oklahoma high school teacher, Daresa Poe, 32, has admitted to engaging in sexual intercourse with an 18-year-old male student, calling it a 'horrible mistake.'
