article_content: When shopping for clothes, most of us prioritize priceâfollowed closely by quality and fitâover ethical concerns about how, where, or by whom garments are made. This trend has contributed to declining sales of ethical clothing: Fairtrade cotton sales, for instance, dropped from 18 million items in 2009 to 12 million in 2010. Last week, however, ethics returned to the spotlight when Rebecca Gallagher, 25, discovered a hand-stitched message sewn into a Â£10 Primark sundress: 'Forced to work exhausting hours.' Found near the care label, the note sparked public outcry. Primark claims no knowledge of how it got there and says there have been 'no other incidents,' but the discovery raises urgent questions about labor conditions in fast-fashion supply chains. So where can consumers shop ethically without breaking the bank or harming the planet? While niche online retailers like fashion-conscience.com, ethicalsuperstore.com, and stylewithheart.com offer genuine ethical fashion, the real power for change lies with major High Street brands. Though terms like 'sustainability,' 'fair practice,' and 'ethical' are widely used, verifying claims is challenging. Tamsin Lejeune, founder of the Ethical Fashion Forum, notes: 'Certain companies are getting serious about their supply chainsâbut every brand operates under its own standard.' Still, informed shoppers can find meaningful progress. H&M leads the pack with its Conscious Collection: affordable pieces made from Tencel (Â£29.99 shirt dress), organic cotton blends (Â£4.99 vests), and partially recycled denim (Â£29.99). The brand consistently ranks highest in sustainability surveys and pioneered materials like organic leather and recycled wool. Its Clevercare labels encourage lower-temperature washing, and it runs a clothing recycling program. Asos supports ethical production through Asos Africaâa line made in Kenya using local fabrics. Highlights include a Â£35 mesh maxi-dress and a Â£12 zebra-print scarf. Zara has joined the Ethical Trading Initiative and is actively working to raise worker wages to meet 'living wage' benchmarks, according to Labour Behind The Label (LBL). As LBLâs Hannah Smith observes: 'Many garment workers must choose between feeding their families and buying shoes. Doubling a T-shirt makerâs wage costs brands as little as 20p per shirtâbut few are willing to sacrifice profit.' Meanwhile, luxury labels like Armani, Versace, Hugo Boss, and Gucci received low ethical scores due to opaque supply chains and heavy reliance on subcontractors with minimal worker protections. Marks & Spencer stands out with ambitious goals: ensuring living wages for workers in Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and India by 2015, banning wool from mulesed sheep, and using Fairtrade and organic cotton and wool across its rangeâfrom Â£5 vests to Â£349 wool suits. Its Shwopping initiative with Oxfam aims to divert a billion UK garments annually from landfills. John Lewis plans to increase UK-based suppliers by 15% and carries Seasalt, a Cornish brand certified by the Soil Association, offering classic Breton tops for Â£29.95. House of Fraser stocks People Treeâthe Fairtrade pioneer worn by Emma Watson and Livia Firthâwith dresses from Â£45 and Orla Kiely designs from Â£75. article_content: Newly released Russian intelligence documents reveal that Albert James, a former federal Labor MP for Hunter, New South Wales, served as a KGB informant during his time in office from 1960 to 1980. Codenamed 'Agent Albert,' James is among several Australians named in the extensive archive of Vasili Mitrokhin, a KGB officer who defected to the UK in 1992 and brought with him thousands of classified files. While it remains unclear what specific information James provided to the Soviet Union, historical records indicate he was a vocal critic of Australiaâs involvement in the Vietnam War and publicly endorsed Fidel Castroâs communist government in Cuba. ASIO files confirm James maintained regular contact with Alexander Ekimenko, a Soviet Embassy official in Canberra whom Australian intelligence suspected of being a KGB officer. A former police officer for two decades before entering politics, James succeeded his father, Rowley James, in the seat of Hunter. He died in 2006 at age 92. Other individuals named in the Mitrokhin archives include Reginald de Bray, a professor of Russian at Monash University (codenamed 'Silver'), and Katerina Clark, daughter of renowned Australian historian Manning Clark. Clark studied in Moscow via an academic exchange program, and de Bray reportedly showed interest in her connections and research activities. The documents, recently made public by the Churchill College Archive in the UK, offer rare insight into Soviet espionage efforts targeting Australia during the Cold War.

article_content: Itâs a Sunday night in Bridgetown, Barbados. On this vibrant Caribbean island â and across the wider West Indies â cricket isnât just a game; itâs life itself. Tonight, fans pack into the historic Kensington Oval, the same ground that hosted the 2007 World Cup final. No international teams are playing, but a local trophy is on the line â and thatâs more than enough to stir the crowd. Amid the cheers, one man moves quietly through the throng: Franklyn Stephenson. Once a rising star, heâs now remembered as the best player to never represent the West Indies â not because of lack of talent, but because of a choice he made 30 years ago. That decision branded him and his teammates as rebels â forever. In 1983, the West Indies cricket team ruled the world. Led by captain Clive Lloyd, theyâd won back-to-back World Cups in 1975 and 1979. Talent flowed like rain across the islands â so much so that they couldâve fielded two world-class squads. Yet, despite their glory, the players earned little. Cricket wasnât a livelihood. Meanwhile, thousands of miles away, South Africa was entrenched in apartheid â a brutal system of racial segregation that jailed activists like Nelson Mandela and silenced dissent with violence. The world responded with sanctions, including a 1970 ban on South Africaâs participation in international cricket. Desperate to keep the game alive, South African officials secretly planned ârebel toursâ â luring overseas players with life-changing sums: up to $150,000 per athlete. England and Sri Lanka sent teams. Then came whispers: Would the mighty West Indies join? Many stars, including Lloyd and Viv Richards, refused. âBlood money,â Richards called it. But others were tempted. Batsmen Lawrence Rowe and Alvin Kallicharran, bowler Sylvester Clarke, keeper David Murray, and 1979 World Cup hero Collis King all accepted. Franklyn Stephenson, then just 23, had turned them down â until the day the team departed. He changed his mind. âCricket can make a difference,â he told himself. âIâm going to be part of that.â On arrival in South Africa, the players expected hostility. Instead, they were mobbed by crowds â tens of thousands of white fans cheering Black heroes from the Caribbean. For many South Africans, it was the first time theyâd seen Black athletes dominate on the field. âThey were seeing blacks beating whites,â wrote journalist Al Gilkes. âThat was the real victory.â But back home, the backlash was brutal. The West Indies Cricket Board banned the players for life. Careers ended. Livelihoods shattered. David Murray lost everything â his job, his home, even his family. He and his wife, forced to flee Australia after giving birth there during the tour, found no welcome in the Caribbean. âPolitics got into it,â he says. Today, Murray drifts, haunted by what he lost. Stephenson now teaches golf in Barbados. But he runs a cricket and golf academy, where a photo of his rebel team hangs proudly. He doesnât regret going to South Africa. He regrets being abandoned. âNobody looked out for us,â he says. Some call them mercenaries. But Stephenson, King, and Murray see themselves differently. âWe werenât fighting someone elseâs war,â says Stephenson. âWe were ambassadors â for our race, our country, our game. If thatâs being a mercenaryâ¦ then yes, I was.â In the end, the tour didnât topple apartheid. But for a few years, in dusty South African stadiums, it cracked open a door. And in the hearts of those who witnessed it â Black and white â it planted a seed.

article_content: A serious security flaw hidden in Android since 2010 could let malicious apps pretend to be trusted onesâlike Google Walletâand quietly steal your passwords, payment info, and personal data without you ever knowing. Discovered by cybersecurity firm Bluebox Security, this vulnerability, nicknamed 'Fake ID,' exploits a weakness built into Android 2.1 and affects nearly every device running older versions of the OS. Although Google says it has already patched the issue and distributed fixes to manufacturers and the open-source project, millions of phones may still be exposed if users havenât updated. Experts warn that downloading apps from outside the Google Play Store dramatically increases risk. Craig Young from Tripwire and Jonathan French from AppRiver both stress that sticking to official apps greatly reduces dangerâand for those stuck on outdated devices, installing a reputable mobile antivirus is a smart backup plan. Bluebox plans to launch its own free scanner to help users check if their phones are vulnerable. While Google claims no malicious apps are currently exploiting the flaw, security researchers caution that unknown threats often lurk unseen. article_content: On the opening day of Wimbledon, Andy Murray picked up right where he left off â comfortably defeating David Goffin 6-1, 6-4, 7-5 to begin his title defense on Centre Court. Though the British No. 1 admitted to feeling butterflies returning to the very court where he claimed Olympic glory and his first Wimbledon crown, his play was anything but tentative. He controlled the match with precision, rarely letting Goffin settle into rhythm. Murray acknowledged the emotional weight of the moment. 'Walking out here brought back so many good memories,' he said. 'I was nervous this morning â but once the match started, I just focused on playing my game.' The crowdâs thunderous welcome when he appeared at 1 p.m. was a powerful reminder of what he means to British tennis fans â a rare, cherished moment after decades without a homegrown champion. Goffin, ranked higher than most expected to challenge Murray on grass, started nervously. He earned a break point in Murrayâs first service game but couldnât capitalize. By 3-0, he was already behind and struggling to find answers. The first set was a masterclass in efficiency: Murray didnât drop a single point on his serve. In the second set, Goffin showed flashes of his elegant grass-court game, but Murrayâs relentless consistency kept him at bay. The Belgian fought harder in the third, stepping forward more often and pushing Murray to deuce multiple times. Still, he couldnât break through. At 5-5, Goffin held a 40-15 advantage â but two unforced errors handed Murray the decisive break. A final ace sealed it, followed by a triumphant fist pump. Watching from the stands were his partner Kim Sears, new coach AmÃ©lie Mauresmo, and his ever-present mother, Judy Murray â all smiling as the Scot moved effortlessly into the second round. 'It was a good start,' Murray said. 'Now itâs time to focus on the next match.'

article_content: In April 2013, a British grandmother named Lindsay Sandiford had her death sentence upheld by a court in Bali after being caught smuggling over 10 pounds of cocaine hidden inside her luggage. The drugs, worth roughly Â£1.6 million, were discovered upon her arrival at the islandâs international airport. Though she was convicted and sentenced to execution by firing squad, the prosecution had not even requested such a severe punishment â a detail that sparked widespread concern. Sandiford, 56, from Cheltenham, claims she was forced into the operation after receiving threats against her sonâs life. Her cooperation with Indonesian authorities led to the arrest of three other British nationals allegedly behind the scheme: Julian Ponder, Rachel Dougall, and Paul Beales. While Sandiford faces death, Ponder received six years, Dougall one year, and Beales four years â a stark contrast that has fueled debate over fairness. Her legal team and the British government argue that her rights were violated during detention. Reports indicate she was denied access to a British consul for nearly two weeks, was interrogated without a lawyer or translator, and was subjected to threats and sleep deprivation. These claims were detailed in an official UK government submission called an Amicus Brief, which urged Indonesian judges to consider her cooperation and vulnerable circumstances before imposing the ultimate penalty. The court, however, ruled that her actions harmed Baliâs reputation as a tourist destination and undermined national anti-drug policies. Despite international outcry and appeals from then-Foreign Secretary William Hague, the verdict stood. Sandiford remains on death row in Kerobokan Prison, where she is held alongside the other convicted Britons. Meanwhile, Dougall is set to be released soon after serving her sentence. The UK continues to advocate for clemency, reiterating its firm stance against capital punishment â a position it has consistently communicated to Indonesian officials.

article_content: More than 2,100 patients died from dehydration or malnutrition in UK hospitals and care homes over the past decade, according to official figures. In 2012 alone, 186 deathsânearly four per weekâwere linked to these conditions, often affecting elderly individuals too frail or cognitively impaired to feed or hydrate themselves. Data from the Office for National Statistics reveals 1,323 hospital deaths and 273 care home deaths caused by dehydration between 2003 and 2013. An additional 499 hospital and 67 care home deaths were attributed to malnutrition. Many more patients were found severely dehydrated or malnourished at the time of death, though these conditions were not listed as the primary cause. Officials acknowledge that illnesses like dementia increase vulnerability, but stress that basic care obligations remain non-negotiable. Norman Lamb, Minister for Care, condemned the failures as 'utterly unacceptable,' noting that care homes are legally required to provide adequate food and drink, and that the Care Quality Commission (CQC) must act swiftly when standards lapse. A Department of Health spokesperson called the situation 'utterly scandalous,' pledging that CQC inspections will now include mandatory nutrition checksâwith financial penalties for the worst offenders. A recent CQC report found that one in ten inspected facilities showed signs of neglect, including patients left without water or assistance eating. article_content: In a royal-themed tearoom in Stanhope, County Durham, owner Anita Atkinson sparked controversy when she asked three elderly women to leave after they refused to stand for the National Anthem. Atkinson, a devoted royalist and Deputy Lord Lieutenant of Durham, runs 'Royal Teas' â a whimsical cafÃ© celebrating the British monarchy with Union Jack furniture, royal memorabilia, and life-size cut-outs of the royal family. Every day at 3 p.m., a musical helium balloon plays the National Anthem, and patrons are encouraged to stand as a nod to the venueâs patriotic spirit. On the day in question, nearly everyone â including four teenagers â rose to their feet. But three women remained seated. When Atkinson asked them politely to stand, one replied, 'Iâm not standing.' Atkinson responded, 'Will you please leave then?' The women departed without paying in full: two settled their bills, while one tossed a pound in change onto the counter, commenting that the coffee was unsatisfactory. Atkinson, 55, insists the tearoom is meant to be lighthearted fun, not a political statement. 'Everyone knows it has a royal theme,' she said. 'We play patriotic music, decorate with royal relics â if they didnât like it, why did they come in?' She noted that the women spoke during the anthem and left with visible dissatisfaction. A lifelong royal enthusiast, Atkinson began collecting memorabilia in 1977 after receiving royal gifts for her 21st birthday during the Silver Jubilee. She once held the Guinness World Record for the largest royal collection â a title since passed to a woman in Australia. Despite her passion, she maintains the tearoom is open to all â as long as they respect its spirit.

article_content: (CNN) â Iranâs finance minister has warned that oil prices could surge as high as $160 per barrel due to sanctions targeting its nuclear program â a forecast made just as the head of the United Nations nuclear watchdog arrived in Tehran for high-level talks.  "We must carefully consider the implications of oil revenues and sanctions on oil sales â who truly benefits, and who suffers?" Shamseddin Hosseini told CNNâs "Fareed Zakaria GPS" in an interview airing Sunday. "Itâs undeniably challenging â but not just for Iran. We can be certain that international oil prices will rise significantly. Is this the most effective strategy?" The remarks came as the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) issued a cautious statement confirming that Director-General Yukiya Amano was traveling to Tehran to discuss "issues of mutual interest" with senior Iranian officials. The visit has sparked speculation that Iran may be preparing to grant IAEA inspectors access to sensitive nuclear sites, potentially clarifying whether it is pursuing weapons-grade enrichment. The talks occur at a critical juncture: Iranâs economy has been severely strained by sanctions imposed by the United Nations, the United States, and the European Union. With 80% of its foreign revenue derived from oil exports, an EU embargo scheduled to take effect in July threatens to inflict further damage. Yet Hosseini argued the sanctions would also harm the EU, which itself faces economic instability. "Oil prices will rise well above $100 per barrel," he said. "Even the International Monetary Fund projects that sanctions could push prices toward $160 per barrel." Hosseini offered no indication that Iran would abandon its nuclear program, which Tehran insists is solely for civilian energy production. "Dialogue is ongoing, but there cannot be hegemony or double standards in how nations like Iran are treated," he said. "If mutual respect and fairness are upheld, we can achieve progress. Otherwise, we will see even greater volatility in global oil markets." Iran and the IAEA held their first meeting in three months in Vienna last week and are scheduled to reconvene Monday. Later this week in Baghdad, Iran will engage in further nuclear discussions with the P5+1 â the United States, France, Russia, China, Britain, and Germany. Regional tensions remain high. Earlier this year, Iran threatened to close the Strait of Hormuz â a crucial oil transit route â if oil export sanctions were enforced. Meanwhile, Israel has hinted it might launch military action to prevent Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons. During periods of heightened tension, oil prices spiked to $110 per barrel. Last week, crude closed at $92.50 per barrel. In March, the IAEA reported a sharp and concerning uptick in Iranâs uranium enrichment capacity. The U.S. and its allies suspect Iran is circumventing inspections and advancing toward nuclear weapons capability â a claim Iran denies. In response, Western nations have imposed severe economic sanctions. On Saturday, leaders of the Group of Eight â the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, and Russia â urged Iran to fully cooperate with the IAEA. In a joint declaration, they welcomed the resumption of talks and called on Iran to take "concrete, step-by-step measures based on reciprocity" to restore confidence that its nuclear program is exclusively peaceful. The G8 also urged Iran to uphold its international obligations regarding human rights and fundamental freedoms, including religious liberty.

article_content: A 3-year-old boy, Shoaib Bali, is recovering after a horrific attack in which his genitals were severed during what authorities suspect was a sorcery ritual. The incident occurred in Peeran Kaliyar, a small village in Uttarakhand, northern India. While playing in a sugar field, Shoaib was ambushed by five men who pinned him down and cut off his genitals with a rusty razor blade. The attackers fled, leaving the bleeding child to stumble home alone. His mother, Gulshan, 25, described the moment she saw him: 'I couldn't believe my eyes. He was covered in blood and in shock. When he fainted in my arms, I thought Iâd lost him.' His father, Salim, 30, searched the field and found the bloody razor blade. 'We know someone took his vital parts for sorcery,' he said. 'They targeted a young boy for this heinous act.' Shoaib was rushed to Shri Mahant Indresh Hospital in Patel Nagar, where pediatric surgeon Dr. Madhukar Maletha performed emergency surgery. 'The injuries were too severe for reconstruction,' Dr. Maletha said. 'We performed a skin graft and will create a new urinary passage using remaining nerves.' Police have arrested five suspects, two of whom are known locally as self-styled religious healers. A spokesperson confirmed they were seen near the scene before and after the attack and that investigators are exploring the sorcery motive. This case follows a similar incident in Rajasthan, western India, where the genitalia of a 17-day-old infant were removed amid allegations of a family feud.

article_content: Bayelsa, Nigeria (CNN) â The stars of African cinema walked the red carpet at the African Movie Academy Awards (AMAA) in Nigeria, highlighting films poised to make an impact on the global festival circuit. The African film industry gathered in Yenagoa, in the Niger Delta region of Nigeria, for the fifth annual âAfrican Oscars.â Founded in 2005 by former lawyer Peace Anyiam-Osigwe, the awards have significantly raised the global profile of African cinema. 'African films have long struggled to gain recognition at most international film festivals,' Anyiam-Osigwe told CNN. 'One of the AMAAâs greatest achievements is that major festivals now view our selections as a trusted curatorial gateway â often picking films weâve highlighted to feature in their lineups.' The first Nollywood film screened by the British International Film Festival was Kunle Afolayanâs 'Irapada,' which won Best Indigenous Film at the AMAA in 2007. This year, 'The Figurine' premiered at Rotterdam and went on to other festivals, while 'From a Whisper' gained international traction after winning at the AMAA. 'The Figurine,' a thriller about a mystical sculpture by Nigerian director Kunle Afolayan, dominated this yearâs ceremony, winning five awards â including Best Picture. Afolayan told CNN, 'It feels incredible â like all our efforts havenât been in vain. Weâve opened a new chapter in African cinema. For me, a powerful story transcends borders â it speaks to any film lover, no matter their language, continent, or skin color.' In its early years, the AMAAs focused primarily on Nigeriaâs booming film industry â known as Nollywood. Today, they have evolved into a truly pan-African event. This yearâs 24 awards included nominations from across the continent. Yet in terms of volume, Nigeria remains the powerhouse of African cinema. According to the UNESCO Institute for Statistics, Nigeria produced 872 films in 2006 â more than double the 485 major feature films produced in the United States that same year. Nollywood films are typically low-budget, often filmed, edited, and released within a month. Most never reach theaters; instead, theyâre distributed as affordable VCDs priced at $1â$2, making them accessible to millions across Africa. But Anyiam-Osigwe credits Nollywoodâs most transformative contribution to its pioneering adoption of affordable digital cameras instead of expensive 35mm film. 'Thereâs a new wave of African cinema driven by the digital revolution â building on what Nollywood started in the early 1990s,' she said. 'Nigeria proved that you can make compelling films without huge budgets. That mindset has spread across the continent â and without it, African filmmaking might not exist at scale.' 'Many older African filmmakers made only one short or feature film in their lives because they couldnât afford to shoot again on 35mm. Now, directors from Malawi, Kenya, and Johannesburgâs âJoziewoodâ have embraced digital â even if some veterans still cling to film.' 'Every African country has its own cinematic voice,' Anyiam-Osigwe added. 'But the stories we tell? Theyâre often the same â love, loss, resilience. Itâs just how we tell them that differs.' Mark Tutton and Christian Purefoy contributed to this report.

article_content: Housekeeper Crescentia Ragonton is accused of stealing a Â£100,000 painting by artist Ed Ruscha from Italian financier Giuseppe Ciardi to pay off her debts and renovate her poorly insulated home, a court heard today. Ragonton, 58, took the artwork titled 'Study for Light' from Ciardiâs home in Chester Square, Belgravia, where she had worked as a housekeeper for six years â often caring for his children. She attempted to sell the painting at Bonhams auction house, estimating its value between Â£80,000 and Â£100,000, but police intervened before the sale could proceed. Prosecutor Guy Saul stated Ragonton admitted to owing Â£15,000 in debts and sought to improve her living conditions, describing her home as 'very cold.' Ciardi, 59, purchased the piece in New York in 2004 for $65,000. A former partner at Morgan Stanley and later founder of hedge fund Park Place Capital, he has endured personal tragedy: his wife Alexandra died in 2005 after being struck by a speedboat while swimming near Porto Cervo, Sardinia. Their three children witnessed the incident. District Judge Michael Fanning called the act a 'significant breach of trust,' noting Ragonton had been entrusted with managing Ciardiâs household. He emphasized that had the theft gone undetected, Ciardi would have suffered a substantial financial loss. Ragonton pleaded guilty to one count of theft. Her defense barrister, Temi Johnson, highlighted her clean record, long employment, and stable family life in Canning Town, East London. Johnson stressed there was no actual financial loss, as the painting was recovered. Ragonton, dressed in a purple checked jacket with her hair tied back, confirmed her details during a brief hearing. She was released on bail with conditions: she must reside nightly at her home address and must not apply for a passport or travel documents. Sentencing is scheduled for a future date at Southwark Crown Court.

article_content: American Airlines has temporarily grounded eight Boeing 757 aircraft after two separate flights experienced alarming incidents where entire rows of seats came loose during flight. The first occurred Saturday on a Boston-to-Miami flight, forcing an emergency landing at New Yorkâs JFK Airport; the second happened Monday on a similar route, also requiring an immediate return to JFK. Passengers reported seats sliding freely across the cabin, creating a dangerous situation as the plane flew through turbulent air. The airline says an internal review suggests the problem may stem from how certain seat models are secured to the floor tracksânot from faulty repairs at any single maintenance site. The FAA has opened an investigation, and American insists safety remains its highest priority. Passengers on both flights were moved to other seats, and alternate planes were arranged to complete their journeys. Sam Mayer, a veteran pilot and spokesperson for the Allied Pilots Association, described the scene as unprecedented in his 24-year career: 'The seats werenât just looseâthey were completely detached. In turbulence, those arenât just inconveniencesâtheyâre projectiles.' He added that the crew had no choice but to request an emergency landing, even though the plane was carrying a full fuel load, making the landing riskier than normal. While American Airlines has been navigating financial hardshipâincluding bankruptcy filings and layoffsâofficials strongly denied rumors linking the incidents to labor unrest. Experts like George Hobica of airfarewatchdog.com warned that even the perception of poor maintenance could drive passengers away: 'If people think itâs unsafe, theyâll book elsewhere. One incident like this can destroy trustâand an airline.'

article_content: President Obamaâs new tax plan offers several thoughtful proposalsâbut it also risks undermining long-term economic growth by taxing saving and investment more heavily, according to economic analysts. One of the planâs strengths is its expansion of the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) for childless low-wage workers. This move, supported by Republican Congressman Paul Ryan, aims to lift more adults into the workforce by providing targeted income support. The plan also addresses a longstanding inequity: the high marginal tax rates faced by secondary earners in married couples. By introducing a second-earner credit and expanding the child care tax credit, Obamaâs proposal reduces the financial penalty on dual-income householdsâa policy backed by evidence showing that affordable child care boosts parental employment, especially among mothers. However, these work-friendly measures are offset by significant tax hikes on capital gains and dividendsâincluding a new rule that would tax capital gains at the time of death. Combined with a top-rate increase of over 4 percentage points (on top of a nearly 9-point hike enacted in 2013), these changes intensify the tax systemâs inherent bias against saving. Under current law, wage earners who spend immediately pay tax only on their income. Those who save and invest pay tax twiceâonce on earnings, again on returns. This double taxation discourages wealth accumulation and reduces funds available for business investment and innovation. While taxing unrealized gains at death could be justified if paired with lower capital gains rates or corporate tax reform, Obamaâs plan leaves the corporate income tax intact. This creates a double penalty on capital without offsetting relief. Funding middle-class tax relief by targeting the savings of high-income households may be politically popularâbut economically, itâs short-sighted. A more sustainable path might involve reducing entitlement growth for high-income beneficiaries or limiting tax breaks for luxury home ownership. As it stands, the plan risks weakening the very engine of future prosperity: private saving and investment.

article_content: A Samurai sword-wielding Mormon bishop helped a female neighbor in Salt Lake City, Utah, escape a Tuesday morning attack by a man who had been stalking her. Kent Hendrix, 47, woke up to his teenage son pounding on his bedroom door, warning him someone was being assaulted outside their home. The father of six rushed out and grabbed the nearest weaponâa 29-inch carbon steel Samurai swordâkept by his bed for martial arts training. Hendrix, a bishop in The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and a fourth-degree black belt in Kishindo martial arts, approached the scene alongside other neighbors. His son remained inside to call 911. Hendrix drew the sword and commanded the assailant to get on the ground. 'His eyes got as big as saucers and he kind of gasped and jumped back,' Hendrix said. 'Heâs probably never had anyone draw a sword on him before.' The suspect, 37-year-old Grant Eggersten, fled on foot but later abandoned his car and escaped in another vehicle. Hendrix retrieved a dropped ChapStick and memorized the license plate, yelling, 'Iâve got your DNA and Iâve got your license plateâyouâre so done.' Eggersten turned himself in to police less than an hour later. He was booked on charges including robbery, attempted burglary, trespassing, and violating a stalking injunction. The victim, a 35-year-old woman, was attacked just after 7 a.m. as she exited her home. Eggersten, hiding behind her carport, knocked her down, stole her keys, and tried to break into her house. She ran for help and sustained minor injuries. Hendrix confirmed this was the first time in his 30 years of martial arts practice that he had drawn the sword in real lifeâand he never swung it, only displayed it to deter the attacker. He praised his 14-year-old son for alerting him and promptly calling emergency services. 'That kind of thing doesnât happen every day,' Hendrix said. 'Our neighborhood is a pretty quiet place.' Hendrixâs wife, Suzanne, confirmed he owns a collection of weapons and has trained with the sword for two decades.

article_content: KATHMANDU, Nepal (CNN) â On Saturday, Nepalâs lawmakers will vote to elect the countryâs first president since becoming a republic. This historic step follows the abolition of a 239-year monarchy after King Gyanendra Shah was removed in 2008. The decision came after Aprilâs elections, which led to the formation of a newly elected Constituent Assembly. However, with no single party securing a majority, the identity of the next president remains uncertain. Though largely ceremonial, the president will formally swear in the nationâs new prime minister. The three main political parties â the Nepali Congress, the Communist Party of Nepal (United Marxist-Leninist), and the Maoists â continue negotiations. The Nepali Congress supports outgoing Prime Minister Girija Prasad Koirala. The UML backs its own leader. But the Maoists, despite winning the most seats, oppose both candidates and are pushing for a non-partisan, non-political figure to serve as president. Journalist Manesh Shrestha contributed to this report.

article_content: Authorities reported that two F-16 fighter jets escorted a small private plane out of restricted airspace near Washington, D.C., following an apparent accidental intrusion that led to the evacuation of key government buildings. The aircraftâa Mooney M20Câentered the restricted zone around 1:30 p.m. and was not in contact with air traffic controllers, according to the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD). NORAD spokesperson Master Sgt. Chuck Marsh confirmed the jets guided the plane to Mount Airy Airport in North Carolina, where it landed safely Saturday afternoon. Secret Service agents met the aircraft upon landing and spoke with the pilot and one passenger, who were en route to visit the pilotâs daughter in North Carolina, per the Boston Globe. Officials believe the pilot became disoriented due to outdated navigation maps. The Transportation Security Administrationâs Ross Feinstein noted on Twitter that the incident appeared to stem from confusion rather than intent. The plane had departed from Westfield, Massachusetts. The U.S. Capitol, adjacent office buildings, the Supreme Court, and the Library of Congress were evacuated during the incident. However, security at the White House remained unaffected. FAA records list Craig Hewitt of Falls Village, Connecticut, as the registered owner, though it remains unconfirmed whether he was piloting the aircraft. As of now, authorities have not determined whether the pilot will face criminal charges or civil penalties.

article_content: While Senator Barack Obama says he will visit Iraq and Afghanistan before the election, he remains consistent in his plan to begin withdrawing U.S. troops almost immediately if elected president. Obama stated on Monday during a two-day swing through Michigan that the rationale for withdrawal is twofold: 'One is to spur greater responsibility from the Iraqis. The second is that weâre spending $10 billion to $12 billion a month in Iraq.' He added, 'The people in Flint, Michigan â whom Iâll be speaking with â want to see some of that investment directed toward rebuilding communities at home.' Obama also expressed concern that the Bush administration might rush to finalize a Status of Forces Agreement that would bind the next president. The war in Iraq is a central issue in the 2008 election, with Obama and Senator John McCain offering starkly contrasting approaches. Obama supports a phased withdrawal, pledging to remove all combat brigades from Iraq within 16 months of taking office. McCain, however, believes U.S. troops should remain until Iraqi forces can sustain a safe, democratic state. He strongly endorses the 2007 troop surge and insists troops must stay as long as necessary. McCain criticized Obama for opposing the surge and questioned his judgment. Obama, in turn, called McCainâs position flawed. On Monday, Obama spoke with Iraqi Foreign Minister Hoshyar Zebari, telling him he looked forward to visiting Baghdad before November. He emphasized that while encouraged by reduced violence, the U.S. must begin withdrawing troops and has no interest in permanent military bases in Iraq. He assured Zebari that an Obama administration would build on existing progress without acting rashly. Zebari did not express alarm over a potential withdrawal, noting that Iraq had made real progress and hoped political reconciliation would follow. Meanwhile, McCain told reporters at his Virginia headquarters that Obama had not visited Iraq in nearly 900 days â a point echoed by the Republican National Committeeâs online countdown timer. McCain argued the campaign should focus on whether to let the surge succeed or repeat past mistakes by setting premature withdrawal deadlines. He also criticized Obama for not meeting directly with General David Petraeus, the top U.S. commander in Iraq: 'How can you draw conclusions without talking to the commander on the ground?' McCain met with Zebari a day before Obama and described their conversation as productive, affirming his view that the surge had succeeded. Recent indicators show improvement in Iraq: U.S. troop deaths reached a five-year low last month, and Zebari reported the lowest level of violence in four years. Analysts Michael OâHanlon and Kenneth Pollack of the Brookings Institution faced backlash last year after returning from Iraq and arguing conditions were better than widely portrayed. Pollack noted that Democratic narratives often treated Iraq as a symbol of Bush-era failure, making it difficult to acknowledge progress under revised strategy. OâHanlon added that Iraqi security forces have improved significantly, but many Democrats remain reluctant to reassess their stance due to Iraqâs symbolic association with Bushâs perceived arrogance and mismanagement.

article_content: Wayne Rooney has responded to criticism from former teammate Paul Scholes, asserting that he is fully fit and eager to feature in Englandâs final World Cup warm-up match against Honduras. Iâm not going to dwell on it. Iâm not interested. Everyone has their opinions â letâs leave it at that. What matters to me is what Roy Hodgson and the coaching staff think.â Rooney broke an eight-month international goal drought by scoring Englandâs opening goal in their 2-2 draw with Ecuador. He is the only outfield player to start both of Englandâs warm-up matches and has trained without any recurrence of the groin injury that ended his Premier League season early. 'I can play in multiple positions,' Rooney added. 'Iâve played on the left before. The manager didnât need to explain the role â Iâve done it many times. Weâve trained hard together â hopefully, we bring that form into the tournament.' Former Manchester United manager David Moyes has backed Rooneyâs inclusion in the starting XI. 'He has to play,' Moyes said. 'He has the ability, the mentality, and the experience. Thereâs too much pressure on him â England havenât performed well in recent tournaments, so expectations shouldnât be unrealistic. But Wayne will be crucial. Heâs in a better place now than last year. He wants to shine â and he will.'

article_content: In a rare public rebuke, EU President Herman Van Rompuy urged the European Court of Auditors to tone down its critical reports on EU spending and instead highlight positive aspects of the blocâs Â£110 billion annual budget. The Court â an independent watchdog that has refused to certify the EUâs accounts for 18 straight years due to persistent concerns over fraud and financial irregularities â has long been a thorn in the side of Brussels. Speaking on Thursday night, Van Rompuy warned that the Courtâs reports are not merely technical documents but powerful narratives shaping public opinion. He pointed out that headlines like 'Yet again, the EUâs accounts have not been signed off' fuel misleading perceptions of widespread mismanagement, even when the underlying issues are more complex. 'Every year, these reports generate headlines that misrepresent the truth,' he said. 'You and I know the reality is more nuanced. Given their impact on public trust, the Court should consider how to encourage more balanced media coverage.' He added that in times of economic uncertainty, fostering confidence in the EU is essential. 'We are all responsible for Europeâs image. We must teach citizens that Europe is not the source of problems â but the solution.' His remarks sparked immediate backlash from British MPs. Conservative MP Douglas Carswell accused Van Rompuy of trying to 'turn a blind eye to dodgy account-keeping.' UKIP leader Nigel Farage went further, asking, 'In which other banana republic would a president publicly demand less exposure of taxpayer waste?' The controversy comes after the Court was informed in June 2013 that its budget would be slashed by 4.2%, raising suspicions that the funding cut and Van Rompuyâs remarks were coordinated efforts to weaken oversight.

article_content: A fiancÃ© faked his own death by phoning his partner and pretending to be his father to deliver the false news â all to avoid his upcoming wedding, it was revealed today. Bride-to-be Alex Lanchester, 23, of Sutton Coldfield, West Midlands, received a phone call months before her wedding claiming that Tucker Blandford, also 23, of Stamford, Connecticut, had died in a car accident. She immediately contacted his parents to offer condolences, but they told her he was alive and well â and she soon discovered he had fabricated his death to escape the marriage. The couple met in August 2012 while studying abroad at the University of Connecticut. Alex worked at the campus cinema in Storrs, 25 miles east of Hartford, where she met Blandford, a set painter, on her first day. She recalled: 'He was such a gentleman â always buying me dinner and beautiful vintage jewelry. I'd never been in love like that before. Every Sunday, he took me out for pancakes. It was so sweet.' To celebrate their anniversary on the 10th of each month, they enjoyed fancy dinners. The thought of returning to England broke her heart. After a year together, Alex began planning her return to the UK â but Blandford proposed. They spoke daily and started making lifelong plans. Alex organized her dream wedding, setting the date for August 15, 2014. She bought a handmade dress from eBay and meticulously planned every detail. She even paid for Blandfordâs flights to the UK to assist with preparations and enjoy a holiday together. 'I went all out, even though I had almost no money,' she said. 'In the weeks leading up to his visit, I was bursting with excitement.' When he called to say heâd booked the venue at their university â the very place they met â she was ecstatic. 'I couldn't think of a more romantic place to tie the knot.' She spent Â£600 on photographers, invitations, and bridesmaidsâ dresses. One week before Blandford was due to arrive, Alex received a chilling call. A man claimed to be Tuckerâs father, saying he had been deeply depressed and thrown himself in front of a car. 'I couldnât breathe. It was absolutely devastating,' she said. After calming down, Alex called back â only to learn from Blandfordâs mother that he was fine and had no idea what she was referring to. Blandford later admitted to the deception, telling reporters: 'Iâm a terrible, awful person. I know I shouldnât have told her I was dead, but I didnât know what else to do.' article_content: Historians have uncovered compelling evidence that Adolf Hitler concealed a vast personal fortune across multiple Swiss bank accounts, contradicting his public image of austere devotion to Germany. Based on his known income streams, scholars estimate he evaded approximately Â£1.75 million in taxes before securing legal exemption through legislation he himself enacted. Mein Kampf became a financial windfall after Hitler mandated that every newly married German couple receive a free copy, funded by taxpayer money. Over 10 million copies were distributed by 1945. In it, he declared all his possessionsâno matter their valueâbelonged to the Nazi Party, and instructed that his relatives receive only enough for a 'simple middle-class life.' The will, witnessed by his private secretary Martin Bormann, was intercepted by Allied forces in May 1945 after a Nazi sympathizer attempted to smuggle it out of Germany hidden in a jacket shoulder pad. The document is now archived at the U.S. National Archives. Bormann disappeared shortly after Hitlerâs suicide and was confirmed dead only in 1973. article_content: In May 2012, Isel Pineda, a heart transplant survivor and former model, went to Brooklyn plastic surgeon Dr. Oleg Davie for a cosmetic liposuction procedure called SmartLipo â a decision that cost her life. Despite having received a life-saving heart transplant in 2004, Pineda was not medically cleared for any procedure requiring anesthesia, let alone invasive body contouring. Yet Davie proceeded anyway, allegedly concealing her full medical history on official forms by falsely marking 'no' to questions about prior hospitalizations. Documents later discovered in her purse revealed she was taking immunosuppressant drugs and had a detailed record of her transplant â proof that Davie could not have missed her condition. Pineda suffered cardiac arrest inside Davieâs office shortly after the procedure began. Emergency responders rushed her to Coney Island Hospital, where she was pronounced dead. Authorities say Davie, who had already been barred by the state health department from performing anything more complex than wart removal or Botox due to a pattern of negligence, ignored these restrictions and prioritized profit over safety. The $3,200 procedure, advertised online as a way to 'lose the wobble,' was a blatant exploitation of a patient whose vulnerability he should have protected. article_content: Palestinian citizens of Israel have faced assaults, harassment, and discrimination since the terrorist attacks by Hamas on October 7, according to a local activist interviewed by Insider. Jafar Farah, director of the Mossawa Centerâan organization advocating for Palestinian rights in Israelâsaid in a Thursday interview that his nonprofit has received a growing number of reports detailing physical attacks, hate speech, workplace discrimination, and bias against Palestinian citizens since Hamas launched its surprise assault on Israel. 'On a daily basis, we receive messages from communities across the country reporting incitement and hate speech directed at them,' Farah said. Farah recounted an incident earlier this week in which Israeli police in Haifa attacked a young Palestinian man with special needsâfor no apparent reason. 'Almost every day, we hear about new cases of physical violence,' he added. In another case, a Palestinian physician at an Israeli hospital reported being accused by a colleague of supporting 'terror.' The Mossawa Center has also documented multiple reports of Palestinian students being harassed on university campuses and workers being fired after unfounded allegations linking them to Hamas. According to a statement issued by the Mossawa Center, Palestinian communities are organizing emergency aid among themselves, fearing that Israelâs national emergency medical services may once again refuse to enter Arab townsâas occurred during prior military escalations. 'Everybody is terrified. We feel like weâre living under a military regime these days,' Farah told Insider. 'We are not the enemy.' Farah emphasized that Palestinian citizens of Israelâcomprising about 20% of the populationâhave long endured systemic discrimination, but that such prejudice has intensified sharply since the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas war. 'There is always some level of discrimination and racism against Palestinian citizens of Israel,' Farah said. 'But when regional conflict erupts, no one acknowledges that we are also victimsâand instead, we become targets.' Palestinian journalist Hanin Majadli wrote in a Friday column for Haaretz: 'If being a Palestinian Israeli is a complex experience in normal times, it is almost impossible now.' 'Since the war began, I and 2 million other Arab citizens are seen as guilty,' Majadli wrote. 'Because we are quiet, or scared, or because we dared to mention contextâor worse, because we spoke about the occupation.' The October 7 attacks by Hamas militants killed more than 1,300 people in Israel and resulted in nearly 100 hostages, according to Israeli officials. The Mossawa Center reported that approximately 15 Palestinian citizens of Israel were also killed in the attacks. Many Palestinian Israelis now live with what Farah calls 'double realities': they fear for their own safety while watching relatives and fellow Palestinians die in Gazaâand they are silenced from expressing grief, lest it be mistaken for support of Hamas. 'There are no Hamas supporters inside the Palestinian community of Israel,' Farah insisted. 'There is a population that wants to treat all of us as if we are Hamas.' More than 1,500 peopleâincluding 500 childrenâhave been killed in Gaza since Israel began its retaliatory airstrikes, which have destroyed residential buildings, universities, hospitals, and mosques, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. 'Our position, at the end of the day, is that this bloodshed must end,' Farah said. The Mossawa Center has called for an immediate ceasefire, peaceful reconciliation between Palestinians and Israelis, and the explicit exclusion of civilians from violence in any future military escalation.

article_content: At 16, a young woman left her farming village to seek work in a distant city. With three younger siblings at home, her parents could no longer afford to keep her in school. Her first job was on a factory assembly line, paying just $50 a month. Over two years, she attended night school, secured a series of secretarial roles, and eventually landed a coveted position in the factoryâs purchasing department â earning over $1,000 a month. She met a fellow migrant, married him, and had two children. Together, they saved enough to buy an apartment for her parents and a used Buick for themselves. Then, leaving her daughters temporarily with her husbandâs family, she returned to the city to work again. 'A person should have some ambition while she is young,' she wrote, 'so that in old age she can look back and feel her life was not lived in vain.' The outline of Lu Qingminâs story is familiar â it could be the tale of any immigrant who crossed oceans to build a better life in America. We honor their struggles and celebrate their transformation. But when I say her name is Lu Qingmin and she lives in China, something shifts. Suddenly, her story is no longer one of hope â it becomes a symbol of oppression under the worldâs largest authoritarian regime, where workers earn less than a dollar an hour and unions are banned. Her agency vanishes; her triumphs are rewritten as suffering. For two years, I lived among assembly line workers in Dongguan, southern China. They worked 11-hour days â often without breaks â while factories routinely ignored minimum wage laws and withheld pay for minor mistakes. Safety violations led to injuries. Ten or fifteen people shared a room; fifty shared one bathroom. Yet these workers did not appear broken. Despite their youth and lack of formal education, they were resourceful, determined, and proactive. Nearly every woman I spoke with had confronted a supervisor over unfair treatment â and won concessions. They studied computers and typing in private classes. They switched employers strategically. They became the primary breadwinners in their families. They pushed their parents to keep younger siblings in school. They delayed marriage and rejected traditional expectations. Factory work in China is not merely a response to poverty â it is a deliberate, informed choice. Surveys show migrant workers are younger and better educated than those who remain in villages. They leave not just for income, but to see the world and grow as individuals. Migration fuels economic growth, social mobility, and progressive values. Remittances are the largest source of wealth creation in rural China. Studies confirm that women who migrate are more likely to choose their own husbands, give birth in hospitals, and demand equality in marriage. By 2025, McKinsey estimates 520 million Chinese will be middle class â most of them former migrants who succeeded in the cities. Acknowledging the real abuses in Chinaâs factories doesnât mean denying their transformative power. Just as Americaâs industrial revolution was marked by both exploitation and opportunity, so too is Chinaâs. Yet today, anyone who speaks of the latter risks being labeled a corporate apologist. After my TED Talk on Chinese factory workers went viral, I was accused of whitewashing slavery. 'You sickeningly try to make it sound like workers want this,' one commenter wrote. Why such outrage? Journalism thrives on extremes â a brawl at Foxconn becomes proof of systemic horror. But ordinary workers who quietly climb out of poverty? Theyâre invisible. And in a climate of deep-seated fear about Chinaâs rise, complexity is erased. The Chinese government is not a democracy â but its policies have lifted hundreds of millions from poverty. We must resist the urge to reduce China to a monolith of oppression. Its workers are not passive victims. They are architects of their own futures. To deny that is not moral clarity â it is intellectual laziness.

article_content: After being granted special permission to skip the U.S. and Brazilian Grands Prix, the Caterham Formula One team has returned to compete in the seasonâs final race in Abu Dhabi. Their comeback was made possible by a crowdfunding campaign that raised Â£2 million â enough to keep the team alive for one last race and attract potential buyers who might rescue it for 2015 and beyond. Heâs particularly focused on the abrupt exit of a consortium of Swiss and Middle Eastern investors in October, who claimed issues with share transfers â a claim contradicted by former owner Tony Fernandes, who says he never received payment. O'Connell, acting as interim team principal, admits he has no more than three weeks to secure a buyer. Otherwise, the team will be permanently shut down. His dual mission: save jobs and recover money owed to creditors. Heâs already begun gathering documents and instructing legal teams to examine whether anyone engaged in wrongful trading or misappropriation of funds. In the paddock at Yas Marina, O'Connell revealed heâs received around 50 expressions of interest from potential buyers. Four appear genuinely committed. One, described as a perfect fit, has requested extra time to finalize a deal â even asking to delay selling the Leafield factory. Another possibility? Wealthy Middle Eastern individuals drawn to Formula Oneâs prestige, eager to join what Bernie Ecclestone calls âthe most exclusive club in the worldâ â though he insists buyers must have solid financial backing. Meanwhile, Caterham operates on a skeleton crew: just 40 staff in Abu Dhabi and five at base, all working for minimal pay as consultants. Two hundred thirty employees were laid off last week. Driver Will Stevens continues to test the car, as the teamâs fate hangs in the balance â one last lap before the lights go out.

article_content: On July 6, 2013, Asiana Airlines Flight 214 crashed at San Francisco International Airport, killing three Chinese high school students traveling to a summer camp. Among them was 16-year-old Ye Mengyuan, who survived the initial impact but was later struck and killed by a fire truck as responders worked to contain the blaze. Footage from the helmet camera of Battalion Chief Mark Johnson reveals a critical breakdown in communication: multiple firefighters spotted Ye lying motionless near the planeâs left wing, covered in fire-retardant foam. Some believed she was deceased, and none informed Johnson of her exact location. Unaware a person was beneath the foam, a fire rig called Rescue 37 â lacking heat-detection technology â drove over her while refilling its tank. The coroner later confirmed Ye was still alive at the time of impact and died from blunt-force trauma. The incident highlights troubling gaps in emergency protocols. Even though other responders saw her, no one relayed the information up the chain of command. Johnson, upon learning of the body moments later, was visibly shaken, asking for a tarp to cover her remains. Two other students â Wang Linjia and Liu Yipeng â also perished. Wang was not found for 14 minutes after the crash; Liu succumbed to injuries days later. All three were top students from China, headed to a Christian summer camp to improve their English before applying to U.S. colleges. article_content: Ed Miliband came under renewed criticism from within his own party after a senior Labour MP openly condemned his lack of clear policies and strategic direction. Graham Stringer, a high-profile backbencher and former government whip, expressed concern over the 'deafening silence' from Labourâs leader and shadow cabinet over the summer. He argued that their failure to set the agenda or challenge the government represented a 'huge missed opportunity,' attributing it to a lack of coherent policies in critical areas like welfare, housing, and education. Stringer emphasized that the real danger to Labour is not a leadership challenge, but the inactivity of Milibandâs senior teamâtraditionally a period when opposition parties press the government while ministers are on holiday. He stated: 'A huge opportunity is being missed. The second worry is that I donât believe members of the shadow cabinet are being lazyâI think it stems from a lack of coherence and clarity in our policies. Itâs not clear what our stance is on welfare, housing, or education.' While acknowledging Miliband isnât expected to reveal the full 2015 manifesto yet, Stringer insisted the public and party deserve clear, well-articulated policy positions. He also noted growing unease among MPs about the shadow cabinetâs inaction, suggesting the perception of party unity is a 'mirage.' His remarks follow a warning from Shadow Health Secretary Andy Burnham, who cautioned that Labour risks defeat unless it presents a compelling economic vision within months, stating voters 'are not convinced we have the answers.' One frontbencher claimed Labour is 'leaping into traps' set by the Conservatives on welfare, the economy, and immigration. Labour has been without an election strategist since Tom Watson resigned amid controversy over union influence. Miliband has yet to appoint a replacement, while the Conservatives have hired Lynton CrosbyâBoris Johnsonâs former campaign managerâand Jim Messina, who led Barack Obamaâs 2012 victory. A recent poll placed Labour at 36%, the Conservatives at 29%, UKIP at 17%, and the Liberal Democrats at 9%. On Radio 4, Stringer urged Labour to consider bringing back veteran strategist Peter Mandelson to strengthen its messaging: 'Labour needs to get the best person. When Peter Mandelson held that position, the party was far more coherent in communicating its message.' Miliband is reportedly planning a frontbench reshuffle in September to build a more dynamic leadership team.

article_content: Graeme McDowell will take a nostalgic trip down memory lane next week to ensure heâs in the right frame of mind for this yearâs Ryder Cup at Gleneagles. The 35-year-old Northern Irishman has added the Wales Open at Celtic Manor to his schedule, returning to the venue where he holed the winning putt in 2010. 'Iâve got so many happy memories there,' he said. 'I also won the Wales Open at Celtic Manor in 2010 and enjoyed my time at the Ryder Cupâit will definitely get the juices flowing.' McDowell secured his place on the European team via automatic qualification, edging out Stephen Gallacher by the narrowest of marginsâa feat that makes him the first player ever to qualify for four consecutive Ryder Cups without a wildcard. 'Iâm the only man to play in the last four Ryder Cups without needing a wildcard pick,' he said. 'Thatâs something Iâm proud of. It makes a difference earning your spot, even if the margin was tiny.' Off the course, McDowellâs year has been extraordinary: he married in September 2013, won the French Open in July 2014, and became a father last week. 'Itâs been a brilliant summerâfor so many reasons,' he said. He watched Gallacherâs final-round charge at the Italian Open with mixed emotions. 'I thought Stevie was going to make it with four or five holes to go. I felt for him when he didnâtâbut I was thrilled when he got a wildcard. It would have been devastating to come so close and miss out, especially with the Cup in Scotland.' McDowell took last week off for the birth of his first child, daughter Vale, and mother Kristin are doing well. He admitted to being distracted during the BMW Championship, finishing well down the leaderboard. 'Itâs not surprising I havenât been at my bestâitâs been a physical and emotional letdown.' With little chance of qualifying for the FedEx Cup finale in Atlanta, McDowell now turns his focus to Wales. Reflecting on his Ryder Cup journey, he said: 'Iâve ridden that rollercoaster. Iâve hit the opening and closing shots, won on both sides of the Atlantic, and been on the losing side.' Though he played a minor role in Europeâs 2012 comeback at Medinah, McDowell is determined to contribute more in 2014. 'Iâm ready to enjoy Gleneaglesâthatâs not always been the case. Last time, I was mentally drained from playing too much beforehand.' Europe captain Paul McGinley hinted earlier this year that the legendary pairing of McDowell and Rory McIlroyââSuper Macsââwill likely reunite at Gleneagles. Their friendship has been strained over the past year due to a legal dispute between McIlroy and their former management firm, Horizon Sports, which also represented McDowell. McDowell, who plans to leave Horizon at yearâs end on amicable terms, said he hopes to rebuild bridges with Rory. 'Where better to start than Gleneagles?' he smiled. 'Rekindling our partnership against the Americans might just heal a few wounds.'

West Ham manager Sam Allardyce said he is not surprised by comparisons between new signing Cheikhou Kouyate and Patrick Vieira following his impressive debut against Tottenham on Saturday. The 24-year-old, who joined West Ham for a reported Â£7 million from Anderlecht earlier this summer, was the Hammersâ standout performer in their narrow defeat, with his pace and power constantly troubling the home sideâs midfield. His new manager was understandably delighted with Kouyateâs first appearance for the Irons. Kouyate was West Hamâs star performer as they fell to a narrow defeat against Spurs. He possesses considerable pace and strength. Kouyate shares many characteristics with Patrick Vieira as a player. Allardyce was impressed by Kouyateâs debut. In his column for the Evening Standard, Allardyce wrote: 'I thought he (Cheikhou) was our man-of-the-match against Tottenham last week, and I, for one, would be delighted if he came close to emulating Patrickâs consistent level of performance. It was a brilliant debutâone you donât see too often in the Premier League. Normally, when players first arrive from abroad, theyâre gasping for air because they struggle with the sheer intensity of our game. Apart from right at the end against Spurs, when he finally took a breather after another powerful run, his fitness was superbâand infectious. The rest of the players will be thinking: 'Come on, Iâve got to step up to his level.' Allardyce hopes Kouyateâs energetic performances will inspire the rest of the squad as West Ham look to bounce back from their loss to Spurs in their upcoming away fixture against the managerless Crystal Palace on Saturday.

article_content: Even though polar bears are perfectly evolved for life on Arctic ice, sometimes nature doesnât go according to plan. In Svalbard, Norway, a massive polar bearâweighing nearly half a tonâwas caught on video wobbling, slipping, and nearly collapsing across dangerously thin sea ice. The scene, captured by local videographer Heinrich Eggenfellner and photographer Svein Wik, unfolded after hours of patient waiting for the bear to emerge from its resting spot. As the animal ventured onto increasingly fragile ice, it stretched out its limbs wide, trying to spread its enormous weight to avoid breaking through. When that failed, it simply punched a hole in the ice and dove into the freezing water, surfacing moments later to shake off the chill. Though polar bears are built for this environmentâwith wide, paddle-like paws designed to distribute their massâtheyâre not invincible. At over 1,100 pounds, even their adaptations canât always counteract the reality of thinning Arctic ice. For the filmmakers, what began as a routine expedition turned into an unforgettable, almost comical glimpse into the raw, unpredictable reality of survival in the wild. 'It was the most extraordinary thing Iâve ever seen,' said Wik. 'You donât just watch a polar bearâyou feel its presence, its struggle, its quiet dignity.'

article_content: In Poland's landmark parliamentary election, three opposition parties collectively won more than 54% of the vote, decisively ending the eight-year rule of the conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party. According to the final results released Tuesday, PiS received just over 35%âenough to remain the largest single party but insufficient to retain its parliamentary majority. This outcome paves the way for a new coalition government led by Donald Tusk, the head of the Civic Coalition and former Polish prime minister (2007â2014) and European Council president (2014â2019). Voter turnout reached nearly 75%, the highest since Polandâs transition to democracy in 1989, reflecting widespread public demand for democratic renewal. The opposition coalitionâcomprising the Civic Coalition (30.7%), the centrist Third Way (14.4%), and the New Left (8.6%)âsecured 248 of 460 seats in the Sejm, granting them a clear mandate to restore judicial independence and reverse PiSâs institutional reforms. Despite losing power, PiS maintained a strong base of support, particularly among older voters and rural communities. Its campaign, which relied heavily on state-controlled media to attack Tusk as a foreign puppet and stoke fears over immigration and LGBTQ+ rights, backfired, galvanizing opposition. Tusk himself received over half a million personal votesâthe highest ever for a single candidate in Polish parliamentary history. The far-right Confederation party, which had hoped to become PiSâs junior partner, gained 18 seatsâup from 11âbut fell short of expectations. A government-initiated referendum on migration and family policy failed to meet the 50% turnout threshold required for validity, as millions boycotted what they saw as a manipulative tool to rally PiS loyalists. In the Senate, the opposition secured a commanding 66 out of 100 seats, further weakening PiSâs remaining influence. President Andrzej Duda, a PiS ally, must convene the new parliament within 30 days and appoint a prime minister. Until then, the outgoing government remains in a caretaker role. While the transition may take weeks, the election signals a profound shift in Polandâs political directionâaway from illiberalism and toward reintegration with European institutions.

article_content: Both candidates vying to become the next New York City mayor have announced their support for adding two new school holidays for Muslim public school students. Democrat and frontrunner Bill de Blasio said Wednesday that it is only fair to grant religious holidays to Muslim students, just as they are granted to Christian and Jewish students. His Republican opponent, Joe Lhota, agreed, stating he has supported this adjustment throughout his campaign. 'We're not going to lose school days,' Lhota said Wednesday. 'We'll extend the school year by two days. But Muslim students will be allowed to have those days off to observe their holidays.' Both candidates support granting days off for New York Cityâs nearly 150,000 Muslim public school students on Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha, the two holiest days in the Islamic calendar. 'The origins of this nation are rooted in people of many different faiths coming together,' said de Blasio. 'Thatâs why we must respect the Muslim faith by providing Eid holidays for children in our schools.' De Blasio noted that, like Hanukkah and Easter, Eid dates shift annually, forcing students to choose between attending school or observing their faith. 'A child who has an exam on a day that coincides with Eid must choose between fulfilling their religious duty or meeting academic requirements â they canât do both under the current system,' de Blasio said at a Brooklyn event for Muslim Americans. In 2006, Eid fell on a day of mandatory state testing. The debate over Muslim school holidays has persisted for years, but three-term Mayor Michael Bloomberg has consistently opposed the change. 'Everybody would like to be recognized,' Bloomberg said in 2009. 'But the truth is, we need more school days, not fewer.' Currently, Christian and Jewish students receive holidays for their religious observances, while Muslim students do not â despite making up roughly 13% of the cityâs public school population. Adding two holidays would raise the total number of school closures per year to 15. State law requires 183 instructional days but does not mandate specific dates. Despite their stark differences on taxes, public safety, and even baseball loyalties, de Blasio and Lhota find common ground on this issue. New Yorkers will vote on November 5 to choose between the two candidates as the city prepares to move beyond Mayor Bloombergâs 12-year tenure.

article_content: Nine rail workers were just seconds from death in Lancashire after receiving no warning that an 80 mph passenger train was approaching, rail accident investigators have said. The workers, operating on a small bridge along the West Coast Main Line in Lancashire, relied on visual and audible warnings due to restricted visibility caused by the trackâs curvature. However, they received no advance alert that an Edinburgh-to-Manchester Airport train was nearing the site. The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) stated: 'They were forced to take immediate evasive action when the train first became visibleâapproximately four seconds before reaching the worksite. Some staff were unable to reach a safe position and pressed themselves against the bridge parapet.' The incident occurred on the afternoon of September 22 this year, south of Hest Bank between Carnforth and Lancaster. The RAIB has launched an investigation into why the warning system failed. The track workers consisted of contract staff and a Site Safety Controller employed by Network Rail (NR). They were packing ballast under sleepers on the up line (towards London) on the small bridge. A Lookout-Operated Warning System (LOWS) was in use to compensate for the restricted view. The LOWS system is designed so that lookouts, positioned on either side of the worksite, operate toggle switches on a LOWS unit, triggering a radio signal to a static unit near the workers that emits both visual and audible alerts. On the day of the incident, two NR lookouts were monitoring the lineâone on each sideâwith the lookout for the up line stationed about half a mile from the site, offering a clear view of trains approaching from the north. The static unit was located close to the workers. The LOWS equipment had been tested and was functioning normally prior to the incident. The RAIB will investigate why no warning was triggered, examining the sequence of events and identifying any safety lessons. Mick Cash, General Secretary of the Rail, Maritime and Transport (RMT) union, said: 'This incident once again illustrates the dangers track workers face daily on Britainâs railways. We have repeatedly raised concerns about the safety of the LOWS systemâthis RAIB report must compel Network Rail to implement a safer alternative.'

article_content: Visitors to Disneyland Paris were told today that safety is 'the number one priority' after a five-year-old boy was seriously injured in an accident on the Pirates of the Caribbean ride. Iban, a boy from Montpellier in southern France, was left 'fighting for his life' after falling from his boat during the ride. The attraction does not use seat belts. According to Julien Kaufman, Vice President of EuroDisney, authorities are investigating the incident. 'Everything will be done to find out what happened,' he said. Emergency services reported that Iban became trapped between the ride platform and the boat, resulting in chest compression. His father immediately jumped out to retrieve him, but was unable to prevent the injury. Fabrice Delin of Codis emergency services confirmed the severity of the injuries. Disneyland Parisâs emergency team provided rapid first aid, and the ride has been temporarily closed while the family is supported. This incident follows a pattern of accidents at the park: in 2008, a 21-year-old suffered head injuries after falling from Crushâs Coaster; in 2011, five riders were hurt on Big Thunder Mountain when fake rocks struck their train; in 2010, a 53-year-old cleaner died after being trapped under a boat on Itâs a Small World; and in 2010, a 12-year-old boy was temporarily paralyzed after riding the Twilight Zone Tower of Terrorâhe later recovered. In January 2024, four people sustained minor injuries when two coaches on the Disneyland Railroad became uncoupled. Opened in 1992 after a costly construction phase beginning in 1988, Disneyland Paris has drawn 16 million visitors annuallyâtwice the number visiting the Eiffel Towerâbut has never turned a profit since opening. In April 2012, it was revealed the park carried Â£1.6 billion in debt, projected to take over a decade to repay. Last month, a petition signed by over 5,000 people accused the park of neglect, citing issues like reheated food, broken attractions, and canceled shows. Disney has not publicly responded.

article_content: On the evening of November 16, 2012, a tragic accident at Knox County Regional Airport in Maine claimed the lives of three close friends and University of Maine students: David Cheney, Marcelo Rugini, and William 'B.J.' Hannigan III. All three were active members of the Lambda Chi Alpha fraternity, with Cheney serving as president and Hanniganârecently certified as a private pilotâat the controls of a Cessna 172. The plane had just become airborne when it collided with a pickup truck that was crossing the runway. Witnesses reported the aircraft climbed briefly to about 100 feet before veering sharply east and crashing into a dense forest 300 yards away, erupting into flames. Emergency responders arrived quickly, but the intensity of the fire made rescue attempts impossible. The truck, operated by a licensed pilot picking up a colleague, was authorized to be on the airfield and equipped with a radio to monitor air traffic. However, investigators are still determining whether the plane transmitted its position prior to takeoff. The aircraftâs registration number was destroyed in the blaze, delaying official confirmation of its identity. All three men were deeply admired on campus: Cheney, a business major; Rugini, an economics student from southern Brazil; and Hannigan, a 2011 civil engineering graduate who loved sharing flight experiences with friends. Robert Dana, the universityâs vice president for student affairs, described their loss as devastating for the entire community. 'They brought great light and energy to our campus,' he said. Fraternity members gathered in solidarity the next evening, with police present to shield them from media intrusion. One friend, Lucas Bernardi, recalled that the flight was meant to be a joyful outingâsomething theyâd done beforeâand that he had been invited but chose not to go. The Woolworth Mansion â once called New Yorkâs most expensive home â is now available to rent for $150,000 per month. Its grand dining room accommodates over fifty guests, making it perfect for lavish entertaining. Built in 1916 by dime store tycoon Frank Winfield Woolworth for his daughter Helena, this French Gothic masterpiece sits between two other mansions he commissioned for his other daughters. Designed by renowned architect Charles Pierpont Henry Gilbert, the 18,000-square-foot home blends historic elegance with modern comforts. In 1995, the property was purchased for $6 million by the late fitness entrepreneur Lucille Roberts, who converted it into a menâs gym. Last year, it was listed for sale at $90 million â a record-breaking price that earned it the title of New Yorkâs most expensive house. Broker Paula Del Nunzio told the New York Daily News: 'Itâs a miracle this house survived with so many original details intact. The owners didnât just restore what they found â they upgraded every system while honoring the buildingâs heritage. This is architecture as art â and thereâs always a market for that.' The limestone faÃ§ade, central foyer, grand staircase, massive fireplace, and elegant powder rooms reflect meticulous craftsmanship. Even after decades of use and renovation, the mansion retains its pre-war grandeur â a rare treasure in modern Manhattan.
